title: How Joe Biden averted a wider war with Iran: Explained in 10 points
text: Ex-US President Joe Biden Former US Middle East coordinator Brett McGurk recounts how Bidenâs administration coordinated with Israel and regional allies to intercept Iranâs unprecedented missile attack in April 2024, while attempting to prevent the crisis from escalating into a regional war. The United States helped avert a wider Middle East conflict in April 2024 by coordinating an unprecedented multinational military effort to defend Israel against Iranâs missile and drone attack, according to former US Middle East coordinator Brett McGurk. In an account adapted from his forthcoming book Brink: Inside the Race to Free the October 7th Hostages, published by The Atlantic, McGurk detailed how President Joe Biden navigated deteriorating relations with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, stalled hostage negotiations, Iranian-backed militia attacks and the threat of direct confrontation between Tehran and Tel Aviv. McGurk, who was closely involved in hostage negotiations alongside CIA Director William Burns, described how the US administration eventually used its military capabilities and diplomatic leverage to contain the Iranian attack and discourage Israel from launching an immediate counterstrike. Here is how Biden administration worked to prevent the crisis from escalating into a wider war. 1. Gaza hostage negotiations stalled as regional tensions escalated According to McGurkâs account in The Atlantic, Biden had asked him shortly after Hamasâs October 7, 2023, attack on Israel to help negotiate a cease-fire and hostage-release agreement. The first breakthrough came in November 2023, when a seven-day truce resulted in the release of more than 100 Israeli hostages, including women and children, in exchange for hundreds of Palestinian prisoners held by Israel. Humanitarian assistance also entered Gaza during the pause in fighting, McGurk wrote. However, negotiations collapsed on December 1 after Hamas refused to release younger women hostages as agreed and instead proposed moving directly to discussions over older male captives. Israel rejected the proposal, and fighting resumed. McGurk said Hamas subsequently demanded a return to the pre-October 7 status quo, including retaining control over Gaza. Israel, under Netanyahu, rejected the possibility of Hamas continuing to govern the territory. By February 2024, the war had entered its fifth month, with nearly 30,000 Palestinians reported killed, including militants, according to the figures cited by McGurk. More than 230 Israeli soldiers had also died, while Hamas continued to hold over 100 hostages. 2. Iranian-backed attacks on US forces pushed Washington towards confrontation While Washington attempted to revive hostage negotiations, attacks by Iranian-backed militias against American forces in Iraq and Syria intensified. McGurk wrote that attacks against US troops had increased sevenfold since October 7 compared with the previous year, with several strikes aimed at killing American personnel. On Christmas Day 2023, three US personnel were wounded in an attack in northern Iraq, one of them seriously. Days later, Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi group began targeting commercial shipping and military vessels in the Red Sea. According to McGurk, Biden subsequently asked him to meet Iranian representatives in Oman through an existing diplomatic back channel. The meeting was intended to communicate Washington's concerns and prevent further escalation. However, the diplomatic effort failed to produce an agreement. On January 28, 2024, an Iranian-supplied drone struck the living quarters of American troops in Jordan, killing three US soldiers and injuring dozens. Biden responded by ordering what McGurk described as the largest wave of American air strikes across Iraq and Syria in more than a decade. The strikes targeted militia infrastructure, including the leader held responsible for the Jordan attack and an Iranian adviser in Baghdad who was supporting the militias. McGurk said the militias subsequently stopped attacking American forces. 3. Biden attempted to bridge differences between Israel and Hamas In February 2024, McGurk returned to Cairo to revive the hostage negotiations with Egypt's intelligence chief Abbas Kamel and Israeli negotiators led by Shin Bet chief Ronen Bar. According to McGurk's account, the discussions initially appeared to have little chance of success because Israel and Hamas maintained fundamentally different positions. Hamas, through its leadership in Gaza, demanded a complete Israeli withdrawal, a permanent cease-fire and the release of all Palestinian prisoners in Israeli jails. Israel rejected these conditions. McGurk and CIA Director William Burns subsequently developed a compromise proposal focused on releasing a humanitarian category of hostages, including women, elderly people and the sick or wounded, in exchange for Palestinian prisoners. The proposal covered more than 30 hostages, including three Americans. In return, Hamas would receive a cease-fire lasting at least six weeks, with the possibility of extending it while negotiations continued over the remaining captives. Israeli negotiator Ronen Bar indicated that Israel could accept the broad framework, McGurk wrote. However, Egyptian intelligence chief Kamel warned that Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar was unlikely to agree. The negotiations eventually stalled again, with Hamas rejecting the proposed compromise and maintaining its original demands. 4. Netanyahu's Rafah offensive threatened to deepen the crisis McGurk's account describes how Israel's preparations for a major offensive in Rafah, southern Gaza, became another obstacle to negotiations. During the February Cairo meeting, Bar informed the mediators that Israel was preparing its largest military operation of the war in Rafah. According to McGurk, Israeli intelligence believed Hamas remained militarily organised in the area, with brigades, battalions and an extensive tunnel network. Rafah was also sheltering large numbers of Palestinians displaced by Israeli military operations elsewhere in Gaza. Bar argued that the only way to stop the planned offensive was for Hamas to begin releasing hostages. During a subsequent meeting in Jerusalem, Netanyahu told McGurk that Hamas's continued presence near Israel's borders posed an existential security concern. The Israeli prime minister also indicated that if a Gaza agreement could not be reached, Israel might consider military action against Hezbollah in Lebanon to secure its northern border. McGurk wrote that Netanyahu was primarily focused on eliminating Hamas's military capabilities and believed that continued military pressure would eventually force Sinwar to release the hostages. The US negotiator, however, remained concerned that military escalation could further complicate the hostage negotiations. 5. US-Israel tensions intensified over the Gaza war By March 2024, Biden was facing growing domestic political pressure over Israel's military operations and the humanitarian situation in Gaza. According to McGurk, the president was under criticism from sections of his own Democratic Party for continuing military support to Israel. Earlier that month, Biden described Israel's planned Rafah operation as a âred lineâ in an interview, saying Israel âmust pay more attention to the innocent lives being lost.â Vice President Kamala Harris also described the proposed Rafah operation as a âhuge mistakeâ and did not rule out consequences if Israel proceeded. However, McGurk wrote that Biden later clarified that his comments concerned how Israel conducted the operation, rather than whether it should take place. The growing differences between Washington and Jerusalem coincided with the collapse of hostage negotiations. On March 18, Biden called Netanyahu and urged him to offer more Palestinian prisoners as part of the proposed agreement. Netanyahu reluctantly agreed, but Hamas did not change its position, according to McGurk. The United States subsequently abstained from a United Nations Security Council vote on a resolution calling for an unconditional cease-fire in Gaza during Ramadan, allowing it to pass. McGurk said Hamas viewed the resolution as a diplomatic opportunity and used Israel's growing international isolation to reinforce its negotiating position. Israeli negotiators eventually withdrew from the talks. 6. Israel's Damascus strike brought Iran and Israel closer to direct confrontation The crisis took a new turn on April 1, 2024, when Israel launched an air strike in Damascus, killing senior Iranian military commander Mohammad Reza Zahedi and several associates. According to McGurk, Zahedi was a senior Iranian officer responsible for proxy operations across Syria and Lebanon, including support for Hezbollah. Before the attack, Israeli military officials had informed McGurk that the operation was imminent. One Israeli official also warned that Iran might describe the targeted building as a consulate, although Israel maintained that it had no evidence that the facility was a diplomatic mission. After the strike, Iran declared that it considered the attack an assault on Iranian territory and vowed retaliation against Israel. McGurk wrote that American intelligence subsequently began receiving reports of Iranian preparations for a large-scale missile and drone attack against Israeli cities. The potential scale of the retaliation alarmed Washington. Iran had traditionally relied on regional proxy groups to confront Israel and the United States, allowing Tehran to maintain some distance from direct military confrontation. However, the planned attack appeared to represent a departure from that approach. According to McGurk, US officials assessed that Iran was preparing to launch hundreds of ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and drones towards Israel. 7. Biden approved US military deployment despite deteriorating ties with Netanyahu As Iran's preparations became clearer, Israel formally requested American military assistance to defend its territory. McGurk described the request as extraordinary because it departed from Israel's traditional military doctrine: We defend ourselves, by ourselves. Israel sought American assistance involving air wings, destroyers and missile-defence systems. At the same time, Biden's relationship with Netanyahu was deteriorating. McGurk wrote that the two leaders had spoken only a handful of times during the first quarter of 2024, compared with nearly 20 conversations during the final quarter of 2023. The relationship further deteriorated after Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer called for elections in Israel and Netanyahu's replacement. Against this backdrop, Biden held a meeting with senior advisers, including Secretary of State Antony Blinken, CIA Director William Burns and national security adviser Jake Sullivan, on April 4. According to McGurk, Biden approved the emergency deployment of additional American military forces to the region on the recommendation of Defence Secretary Lloyd Austin. The president also discussed whether the United States should threaten to suspend military assistance to Israel to pressure Netanyahu into ending the Gaza war. However, Biden questioned the consequences of such a move while Israel faced attacks from multiple directions and hostages remained in Hamas captivity. âWeâre on the side of Iran?â he asked rhetorically, according to McGurk. 8. Biden confronted Netanyahu and linked Iran's defence to ending the Gaza war During the April 4 telephone conversation with Netanyahu, Biden expressed frustration over Israel's handling of the humanitarian crisis and the continuing military campaign in Gaza. According to McGurk, the president opened the call by asking: âBibi, man, what the fuck are you doing?â Biden warned that the United States could withdraw military assistance, while Netanyahu responded that Israel would defend itself even without American support. The discussion also covered the killing of seven World Central Kitchen aid workers in an Israeli drone strike in northern Gaza on April 1. Biden demanded concrete steps to improve humanitarian access, including opening additional crossings into northern Gaza. When Netanyahu attempted to explain Israel's preliminary assessment of the incident, Biden interrupted him. âI donât want to hear it, Bibi.â According to McGurk, Biden then made clear that the United States would help defend Israel against Iran but expected immediate efforts to end the Gaza war and secure the release of hostages. âThatâs the deal, pal.â Following the call, the White House issued a statement warning that US policy would be determined by its assessment of Israel's immediate actions regarding civilian harm, humanitarian suffering and the safety of aid workers. At the same time, the statement reaffirmed American support for Israel against Iranian threats. McGurk described this as the central dilemma confronting the Biden administration: Washington wanted to pressure Israel over Gaza without weakening its defence against Iran. 9. US-led multinational military operation intercepted Iran's unprecedented attack On April 13, 2024, Iran launched its first direct large-scale attack against Israel from its own territory. According to McGurk's account, the attack began at approximately 3:30 pm with around 200 drones, followed roughly 90 minutes later by 30 cruise missiles. Iran subsequently launched more than 100 ballistic missiles in multiple waves. The attack was designed to overwhelm Israeli air defences by ensuring that drones, cruise missiles and ballistic missiles arrived around the same time, McGurk wrote. The United States had spent the preceding 96 hours strengthening Israel's defences, deploying additional military assets and coordinating with Arab and European countries. During the attack, American fighter aircraft intercepted Iranian drones over Syria, Iraq and Saudi Arabia, while US Navy destroyers and regional air-defence systems helped counter incoming threats. McGurk described how US and Israeli defence systems worked together to intercept the incoming projectiles. Israel's Arrow systems engaged ballistic missiles at high altitudes, while American destroyers fired SM-3 interceptors to destroy incoming threats above the atmosphere. US Army Patriot batteries across the Middle East were also placed on alert. According to McGurk, American pilots Lieutenant Colonel Kevin Murphy and Major George Welton, along with their squadron, shot down around two dozen Iranian drones. The operation involved American military forces working alongside Israeli forces and a coalition of European and Arab countries. As the attack unfolded, General Erik Kurilla, who was overseeing US military operations, informed Biden that the number of ballistic missiles launched had increased through successive waves. McGurk recalled that the Situation Room tracked more than 100 Iranian ballistic missiles heading towards Israel. Despite the scale of the attack, the combined air-defence effort appeared to have prevented major damage. US military officials initially reported no confirmed impacts, while Israeli authorities subsequently reported no significant impacts. McGurk noted that one young girl in southern Israel was wounded by falling shrapnel. The successful interception prevented the immediate military consequences that could have triggered an Israeli retaliatory strike against Iran. 10. Biden urged Netanyahu to avoid retaliation and contain the conflict Following the interception operation, the immediate challenge for Washington was preventing Israel from launching a major retaliatory attack against Iran. According to McGurk, Biden wanted Netanyahu to recognise the success of the defensive operation and avoid turning it into a broader military confrontation. The president asked for Netanyahu to be brought onto a telephone call. When Netanyahu initially requested 30 minutes before speaking, Biden expressed frustration, asking whether the Israeli prime minister understood that the United States had just helped save Israel. National Security Adviser Jake Sullivan and his deputy Jon Finer subsequently prepared talking points recommending that Israel respond in a way that inflicted few casualties and prevented further escalation. During the conversation, Biden acknowledged Israel's right to respond but urged Netanyahu to coordinate with Washington and ensure that any action was designed to deter Iran rather than escalate the conflict. âTake the win,â Biden said. Netanyahu remained noncommittal, arguing that Iran needed to be taught a lesson. However, both leaders agreed that their military teams would discuss possible responses. McGurk wrote that the Biden administration subsequently received another warning from Tehran against supporting Israel in a retaliatory operation. Iran's UN mission also issued a public message stating: âUS MUST STAY AWAY!!â The immediate confrontation eventually subsided, although tensions between Israel and Iran continued. The following morning, Biden spoke with the American pilots and military commanders involved in defending Israel, including Murphy and Welton's squadron. Recalling the operation, Biden told the pilots: âThe only reason weâre not in a major war right now is because of what you did. I mean it, guys. Thank you, thank you, thank you. You saved the world; I mean it. God bless you.â According to McGurk, the episode demonstrated how American military coordination, regional cooperation and direct diplomatic engagement helped prevent Iran's unprecedented attack from triggering a wider regional war. However, the underlying Gaza conflict, stalled hostage negotiations and tensions between Washington and Jerusalem remained unresolved. This article is based on Brett McGurk's first-person account published in The Atlantic, adapted from his forthcoming bookBrink: Inside the Race to Free the October 7th Hostages. title: Gaza war could have ended a year earlier, says ex Israeli hostage negotiator
text: Ex Israeli hostage negotiator revealed that the Gaza war could have been concluded a year prior. Former Israeli hostage negotiator Major General (retd) Nitzan Alon has said Israel could have ended the Gaza war about a year earlier and secured the release of all its remaining hostages without significantly compromising its other strategic objectives. According to Al Jazeera, Alon made the remarks during a Washington Institute for Near East Policy webcast on October 2, arguing that Israel could have reached the position it ultimately achieved âmuch earlier, maybe a year earlier or soâ. He said the prolonged war may have cost the lives of hostages who could otherwise have been brought home alive. Alon, who served as the Israeli military's point person for hostage negotiations during the war, said Israel's insistence on achieving âtotal victoryâ over Hamas before accepting a comprehensive deal was based on a false premise. He argued that the October 2025 ceasefire and hostage agreement demonstrated that Israel could have achieved its broader strategic objectives while reaching a deal much earlier. Alon said the decision to continue the war also had a human cost, arguing that an earlier agreement could have brought some hostages home alive and potentially saved thousands of lives on both sides. Watch âRetake Bab El-Mandebâ: MBS Preps 100,000 Troops Against Iran Ally To Secure Red Sea Route | Report He said Israel âcould have and should haveâ shortened the war and returned the hostages earlier. The October 2025 ceasefire agreement between Israel and Hamas came into effect on October 10, 2025, under a US-backed plan aimed at ending the Gaza war and securing the release of the remaining Israeli hostages. Under the first phase of the deal, Hamas agreed to release all 20 living Israeli hostages, while Israel agreed to release Palestinian prisoners and detainees and withdraw its forces to agreed positions in Gaza. The October 2025 deal came nearly two years after the October 7, 2023 Hamas-led attack on Israel, in which 251 people were abducted and taken to Gaza. The attack killed more than 1,200 people, according to Israeli figures, triggering Israelâs military campaign in Gaza and a prolonged effort to secure the release of the hostages. title: Can Jared Kushner broker Gaza peace while investing in Israel? His billion-dollar ties face scrutiny
text: By October 2025, Kushner was deeply involved in the administrationâs Middle East diplomacy. Jared Kushner has emerged as an important figure in the Trump administrationâs efforts to negotiate an end to the Gaza war. At the same time, his private equity firm, Affinity Partners, is the biggest shareholder in an Israeli financial company that has invested in businesses supplying equipment to Israelâs military, a CNN investigation has found. Affinityâs investment is in Phoenix Financial, a major Tel Aviv-based financial firm. CNN traced Phoenixâs investments using Israeli financial disclosure records and found that it has put hundreds of millions of dollars into Elbit Systems, Israelâs largest arms manufacturer, as well as at least eight other companies that supply equipment to the Israeli military. The businesses identified include companies involved in drones, warships, tank equipment and machinery used for demolition. Affinity does not directly own shares in those nine military-linked companies. However, because it owns a large stake in Phoenix, it can benefit financially if Phoenix profits from those investments. All nine companies identified by CNN saw their stock prices rise last year. Several also said the war in Gaza had increased demand for their products. Phoenixâs holdings in the nine companies were worth more than $456 million, according to CNNâs investigation. Kushnerâs investment grew as he entered diplomacy Affinity first bought a stake in Phoenix in July 2024. In January 2025, shortly before Donald Trump returned to the White House, the investment firm doubled its stake, making it Phoenixâs largest shareholder. By October 2025, Kushner was deeply involved in the administrationâs Middle East diplomacy. He had been involved in negotiations between Israel and Hamas and appeared in Tel Aviv following the release of hostages. This created an unusual situation in which Kushner was involved in efforts to negotiate an end to a war while his investment firm continued to hold a major financial interest in an Israeli company whose investments included businesses connected to the military campaign. CNN found no evidence that Kushner directly influenced Phoenixâs investment decisions in the companies linked to Israelâs military. Kushnerâs lawyer said he is not on Phoenixâs board, has never held a management position there and does not decide where the company invests. However, CNN reported that Kushner previously said he had regular discussions with Phoenix executives and met with the companyâs team every few weeks. His lawyer said Kushner has reduced his contact with Phoenix management since becoming more involved in public service and diplomatic work. Affinity has made a substantial return Kushnerâs firm has already made significant money from its Phoenix investment. In July this year, Affinity sold around a quarter of its Phoenix stake for more than $340 million. CNN reported that this represented a return of more than five times the firm's original investment. Affinity remained Phoenixâs largest shareholder, with a 7.4% stake worth more than $1 billion at the time. Kushner has openly defended his approach of combining business and diplomacy. He has argued that economic cooperation can help bring Israelis and Arabs together and ultimately contribute to peace. âWhen you get an Arab and Israeli together and they start talking about a business opportunity, they forget about everything else and then they realize that thereâs a lot of similarities,â Kushner told the âNo Priorsâ podcast in September last year. âMy investors from the Middle East are now looking at Israel, and theyâre saying, âWait a minute, maybe thereâs a benefit to having these wars done,ââ he added. Critics question the overlap The combination of Kushnerâs private investments and his role in Middle East diplomacy has prompted criticism from government ethics experts. Cynthia Brown, chief ethics counsel for Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, said people who stand to benefit financially from government policy should not also be involved in making those policy decisions. âThere are always people who profit from war or government policies. The difference is that the people profiting should not be the people making the decisions to make that policy. And that is what is happening here,â she said. Kushner has operated as a volunteer envoy rather than taking a formal government position. CNNâs investigation says this has meant his finances have not been subject to the same disclosure requirements that would apply to someone holding an official government job. title: 'October 7 attack equal to sixteen 9/11s': Israeli PM Netanyahu in UN speech
text: He also defended Israel's military action against Iran Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack was, in proportionate terms, equivalent to 16 September 11 attacks in the United States. Recalling the attack, Netanyahu said Hamas militants had killed about 1,200 people in Israel, including civilians, and abducted 251 others. âThese Hamas monsters, they slaughtered Holocaust survivors. title: 'Gaza on verge of exploding': Egypt spy chief warned Israel of Hamas escalation before Oct 7
text: File photo: Memorial dedicated to the victims of the deadly October 7 attack on Israel by Hamas from Gaza Egyptâs intelligence chief Abbas Kamel travelled to Israel days before the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack and warned Israeli officials that Gaza was heading towards a dangerous escalation, according to a report by The Atlantic. Kamel arrived at Ben Gurion Airport on September 26, 2023, in a chartered plane linked to Egyptâs intelligence service, according to the report. His visit came as Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and other leaders were marking the 50th anniversary of the Yom Kippur War, the surprise attack by Egypt and Syria that Israel has long treated as a lesson in intelligence failures. According to Israeli, Egyptian, Arab, US and European officials who were briefed on the visit after October 7, Kamel told Israeli officials that Hamas appeared to be preparing for a major attack. He urged Israel to make economic concessions to Hamas to prevent the situation from spiralling. One former Israeli official later briefed on the meeting told The Atlantic that Kamelâs message was essentially that Gaza was on the verge of exploding if Israel did not change course. However, Kamel did not provide a specific date or details of the multipronged attack that Hamas would launch less than two weeks later. The Egyptian plane remained at Ben Gurion Airport for about 67 minutes before returning to Cairo, according to an Israeli airport-authority flight log. It remains unclear exactly which Israeli officials Kamel met during the visit. What Israel did with the warning remains unclear The report said officials from seven countries believed the visit should have raised alarms within Israelâs senior leadership. Netanyahuâs office, however, denied after the October 7 attack that the prime minister had received warnings from Egypt. Tzachi Hanegbi, who was then head of Israelâs national-security council, also denied to The Atlantic that Kamel had visited Israel or delivered an Egyptian warning. The September 2023 visit was not the only warning Israel received. According to The Atlantic , Egypt continued raising concerns about Hamas in the days before October 7, while the UAE's president Mohamed bin Zayed also warned Netanyahu about the possibility of a major attack after receiving intelligence from Egyptian and Palestinian sources. A UN envoy had publicly warned on September 27 that the situation around Gaza could have âgrave consequencesâ, while international negotiators were trying to prevent an escalation. Gaza tensions were already rising In the weeks before the attack, tensions around Gaza had been increasing. Qatar had frozen fuel deliveries to Gaza, while Hamas called for demonstrations at the Erez border crossing. Israel closed the crossing in September after protests. Around 18,000 Gazans had permits to work in Israel, and their inability to cross added to tensions. Egyptian, Qatari and UN negotiators subsequently worked to restore calm, with discussions involving work permits, fuel supplies and other measures. Those efforts temporarily eased tensions. Hamas agreed to pull people back from the border fence, while Israel agreed to reopen the Erez crossing and restore a medical-supply line into Gaza. But, according to negotiators cited by The Atlantic, Hamas was using the talks to buy time while continuing preparations for its attack. The report also said Egypt continued to raise alarms up to two days before October 7. Most of the warnings did not contain a date, target or method of attack, but US, Israeli and Egyptian officials described them as frequent and persistent. The October 7 Hamas attack killed about 1,200 people, primarily civilians, and resulted in 251 people being taken hostage. Israel subsequently launched its military campaign in Gaza. The extent to which the warnings could have changed the outcome remains impossible to determine. But the newly reported details of Kamelâs visit add to the continuing questions over what Israeli officials knew before October 7 and how those warnings were assessed. You use AI every day. title: Israel elections, West Asia wars & Bibiâs last gambit
text: Israeli PM Benjamin Netanyahu meets Yaniv Hayun, one of the Israeli passengers who managed to subdue the co-pilot of flydubai flight FZ1073, who had stabbed its captain, before pulling up the jet's steering control to right it The miraculous survival of Israeli passengers on the flydubai flight that saw an attempted hijacking and potential terror plot â thwarted only by the quick thinking of Indian Captain Smit Machchhar and the passengers â has become the latest hot button issue in Israelâs upcoming Oct 27 polls. Even before the high-altitude drama, the election was shaping up to be a pivotal one, not just for Israel but also the wider West Asia. For, the polls are taking place at a time when US and Iran are still engaged in war â a war Tel Aviv started together with Washington but now seems to have quietly exited â Strait of Hormuz is still not fully open for oil and cargo traffic, and Israel itself is militarily mobilised on four fronts â Gaza, Lebanon, Syria, and West Bank. Plus, these are the first polls since the Oct 7 Hamas attack on Israel that appears to have fundamentally changed Israeli society. Hereâs the lowdown on the Oct 27 polls, the key players, and the issues animating Israeli voters. Lion of Judah The flydubai incident is literally godsent for Netanyahu. He and his Likud Party have been consistently trailing in opinion polls. But ever the political wizard, Netanyahu is approaching the polls on the front foot. He knows the election will essentially be a referendum on his handling of Israelâs security situation since Oct 7. Thus, he is presenting himself as the only leader who can guarantee Isrealâs security. And flydubai just exemplified his long-running narrative that Israel still isnât safe, there are enemies everywhere, and only a strong leader like him can lead the country. His tactic? Go on the offensive against any hint of criticism of Israelâs policies â be it at the UN General Assembly (where Netanyahu basically delivered a campaign speech defending his govtâs record) or blasting New York mayor Mamdani. In doing so, Netanyahu is using an old political trick: fuse his image with that of Israel. Thus, criticising him would be seen as criticising Israel. But Bibiâs campaign isnât without headwinds. The Challenger Netanyahuâs main challenger in these polls is Yashar Partyâs Gadi Eisenkot, a former Israeli army chief of staff. Eisenkot was once No.2 to former PM hopeful Benny Gantz. But he launched Yashar in Sept 2025, months after leaving Netanyahuâs emergency coalition formed after Oct 7. The war in Gaza is very personal for Eisenkot â he lost his son Gal two months into the fighting. Eisenkot has sought to build a centrist coalition, consolidating opposition votes, while also indicating openness to those who are part of the Netanyahu coalition. A poll projection, published this week, showed the opposition bloc led by Eisenkotâs Yashar winning 54 seats in the 120-member Knesset. Netanyahuâs governing bloc was down to 50 seats. TOI Explains Can Eisenkot pull off an upset? Difficult to tell. Eisenkotâs coalition, should it perform per the poll projections, will still be short of the 61-majority mark. Netanyahu, in fact, could be betting on this. He rode out a similar situation between 2018 and 2022, when Israel had five elections. That saw Netanyahu repeatedly frustrate the opposition, eventually returning to power with the most right-wing govt in Israelâs history. So, Netanyahuâs strategy is simple. If he is not getting a majority, make sure the opposition doesnât get one either. This will see Israelis head back to polls, and run the whole thing again. Netanyahu is banking on the fact that people will get tired and conclude thereâs no alternative to him. The Arab dilemma Thatâs the other problem for the opposition. The only way it can cobble together a clear majority is with the support of Arab-led parties. However, in the post-Oct 7 scenario, when Israeli society is so polarised, tying up with Arab parties is kryptonite for anyone vying to form govt. Even if there is no formal alliance, any opposition bloc that relies on votes of Arab parties in the Knesset will be meat for Netanyahu. The latter is already questioning the credibility of the opposition to form govt, saying can Israelis really trust a coalition that would potentially need the support of Arab parties. Will the results impact geopolitics? The regional scenario will remain much of the same, no matter who forms the next Israeli govt. At least in the near term. The divisions within Israeli politics are more on internal issues â corruption charges against Netanyahu, establishment of a state commission of inquiry into Oct 7 failures, judicial reforms, mandatory conscription for the ultra-orthodox Haredi, and the high cost of living. Those looking to unseat Netanyahu see the same threats from Hamas, Hezbollah, and Iran. Only their approach may differ, to a moderate degree. What about Israelâs relations with US? This may be the trickiest issue. Following Israelâs post-Oct 7 wars in Gaza, Lebanon, and West Bank, criticism of Israel and Netanyahuâs govt has grown in US, both on the political left and right. Even MAGA supporters are questioning the unquestioned Washington support for Tel Aviv. Netanyahu essentially believes that US has no choice but to back Israel. Washington, long dependent on Israel to carry out its West Asia policy, may finally be looking to pull back, and allow other allies in the region â Saudi Arabia, UAE, Qatar â to play a bigger role. This would mean that the Abraham Accords are not just a template for Arab-Israeli relations, but also a template to balance against Israel in West Asia. You use AI every day. title: 'Any more moral cowards who haven't yet left the hall?' UN delegates walk out as Netanyahu begins speech
text: âMoral cowardsâ: Netanyahu hits out at UNGA delegates who walked out during his speech Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu used his address to the 81st United Nations General Assembly on Thursday to defend Israelâs military actions against Iran and Hamas, praise US President Donald Trump and attack critics including New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan. Netanyahuâs speech was marked by a walkout by dozens of delegates as he took the podium. He responded by calling those who left âmoral cowardsâ and continued his address to a hall in which many seats were visibly empty. Supporters in the viewing gallery cheered and applauded Netanyahu during parts of the speech. âNo greater partner than President Trumpâ Netanyahu strongly praised Trump for his support of Israel and said the two countries had acted together against threats posed by Iran. "In this battle against the barbarians, we've had no greater partner than President Trump. I thank him for his bold leadership. He boldly confronted an enormous danger to America, Israel, and the world...Israel and America acted together, not only to protect ourselves, but to save civilization," Netanyahu said. He also credited US-Israeli cooperation for Israelâs military campaign against Iran, saying the two countries had acted to protect themselves and the wider world. Netanyahu calls Iran strike âone of the easiest decisionsâ Defending Israelâs military action against Iranâs nuclear facilities, Netanyahu said the decision to launch the operation had been difficult but necessary for Israelâs security. "...Devastating Iran's nuclear facilities was hard. It was very hard to do. But for me, it was one of the easiest decisions I've ever had to make as prime minister. Because if we hadn't done it, we'd all be dead. Now, you want to hear the ultimate irony? In defending itself, Israel is also defending many of the countries whose delegates just left this hall. Many of their leaders even thank us privately for taking out Iran's nukes. It's hard to imagine more mind-blowing hypocrisy, but that's exactly what it is," he said. The remarks came amid continuing tensions over Israelâs military campaign against Iran. Netanyahu has repeatedly framed the operation as an effort to prevent Iran from developing a nuclear weapons capability. âSeven-front warâ: Netanyahu lists Israelâs adversaries Netanyahu described Israel as having fought what he called a âseven-front warâ over the past three years, listing Hamas, Hezbollah, the Houthis, Iran, Iran-backed militias in Iraq and Syria, and Palestinian militants in the West Bank. "For the past three years, our heroic soldiers have fought day in and day out in a seven-front war. Do you know any other country the size of New Jersey, capable of fighting a seven-front war? Seven fronts â Hamas, Hezbollah, the Houthis, Iran, militias in Iraq, militias in Syria, Palestinian terrorists in Judea and Samaria; they all ganged up on us to wipe us off the face of the earth," he said. Netanyahu said Israel had responded by launching military operations against those groups. "They failed. Because instead of collapsing, we delivered crippling blows to all of them. With our great American friends, we crushed Iran's army, navy, air force and nuclear facilities. Israel hammered Hamas. We pummeled Hezbollah," Netanyahu added. Netanyahu holds up pager while referring to Hezbollah During his speech, Netanyahu held up a pager while referring to Israelâs 2024 operation against Hezbollah. He said the groupâs leadership had suffered major losses and referred to the pager explosions that targeted members of the Iran-backed group in Lebanon and Syria. âYou remember the beepers? Remember these things? Remember them? Well, I can tell you this: Hezbollah certainly remembers them...Hezbollah's leaders, dead. Their spirit, broken. The arch terrorists, the worst mass murderers on earth, not only killing Israelis, killing Americans, killing Brits, killing citizens of hundreds, dozens of countries...They're all gone too. The remaining terrorists are desperately trying to regroup. Every day, they try to murder our people. And in particular, they try to murder our people in our historic homeland, in Judea,â the Israeli PM said. The pager attack in September 2024 involved remotely detonated pagers used by Hezbollah members and killed and wounded people across Lebanon and parts of Syria. Netanyahu rejects colonialism accusations Netanyahu also defended Israelâs territorial policies and rejected accusations that Israel was pursuing colonialism. He invoked Jewish historical ties to the Golan Heights while criticising countries including Britain and France. "...We weren't in Gaza. We weren't on the Golan Heights. The Jews have been on the Golan Heights since the days of Moses. You can read it in the Bible. On the eve of the Six-Day War in 1967, we weren't in any of these places. We were in a tiny sliver of land. We still are. That is equal to about one-third of 1 % of the landmass of the entire Arab world. Yet they accuse Israel, tiny Israel, of colonialism, some colonialism. And who's accusing us? Well, among them are people in Britain and in France. ..Colonialism gave us a break. Another lie,â Netanyahu further said. Netanyahu attacks Qatar and Erdogan Netanyahu accused Qatar and Turkey of spreading what he described as false narratives about Israel and criticised their relations with Hamas. "Several foreign countries have spent untold billions to spread lies about my country. The first to do so was Qatar...Their goal was clear. Brainwash young minds to hate Israel, hate America, hate the West. This is the same Qatar that hosts the Hamas butchers of October 7th. Now the latest country to become a super spreader of anti-Semitic lies is Turkey. Erdogan is a tyrant. He also hosts the Hamas terror chiefs. He's murdered thousands of Kurdish civilians. He denies the Armenian genocide. He jails journalists and opposition leaders. In fact, I think he holds the world's record on this, and that's a tough call. But I think he's number one," he said. Netanyahu clashes with Mamdani over Gaza allegations Netanyahu devoted part of his address to Mamdani, accusing the New York mayor of contributing to an environment in which Jewish residents feel unsafe and of associating with people who have expressed support for Hamas. "Mr. Mamdani, since you were elected mayor of this city, many Jews no longer feel safe in New York. They talk to me. They tell me, âThis isn't the city we remember. It changed so quickly.â You praise criminals convicted of supporting Hamas. You count as friends people like Hasan Piker, who said America deserved 9/11. âAmerica deserved 9/11.â Some friends you have. You invited to your home a Palestinian journalist who filmed Hamas terrorists beating and torturing Israeli hostages, and later admitted that he refused to publish the videos in order to protect, you guessed it, the terrorists," he further said. He also accused Mamdani of attempting to prevent him from attending the UN and rejected allegations that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza. "Your wife liked a post praising the October 7 massacre. She liked another post saying Tel Aviv shouldn't exist. You refuse to condemn any of that. You falsely and repeatedly accuse Israel of genocide. Mr. Mamdani, you try to stop me from coming here. You tried to silence me. Well, you can't silence me. You can't silence the truth. And here's the simple truth. Here's a simple truth: Israel didn't commit genocide; Israel prevented genocide," he said. Mamdani has repeatedly criticised Netanyahuâs conduct of the Gaza war and previously referred to him as a âwar criminalâ. He has also disputed Netanyahuâs characterisation of his criticism of Israel as antisemitism. Dozens of delegates walk out as Netanyahu begins speech The Israeli prime ministerâs address began with a visible protest inside the General Assembly hall, with dozens of delegates walking out as he approached the podium. The chair repeatedly called for order as Netanyahu began speaking. Netanyahu directly addressed those who had left, saying: "Before I begin, just a quick announcement: if there are any other moral cowards who havenât yet left this hall, please do so now. Thank you very much." He later argued that Israelâs actions against Iran had also benefited countries whose representatives had walked out, claiming some foreign leaders had privately thanked Israel. Netanyahu urges Jews to âraise your head highâ Netanyahu also spoke about what he described as rising antisemitism and called on Jews around the world to remain confident in the face of threats. "The anti-Semites of the world want to terrify our people. I have news for them: the days when Jews were defenseless victims, marched to the slaughter, those days are over. Today, we have a state. Today, we have an army. Today, we have a people ready and willing to defend ourselves. Today I have one message for Jews around the world: raise your head high, be proud, be confident, don't be intimidated. Stand up. Everyone else who wants to defend truth and justice, join us in standing up to the barbarians who threaten our common civilization,â he said. Netanyahuâs address combined a defence of Israelâs military campaigns with attacks on international critics, while placing the US-Israel partnership and the confrontation with Iran at the centre of his message. Supporters in the viewing gallery gave him a standing ovation at the conclusion of his speech. You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

title: Will the long shadow of Oct 7 scuttle Bibiâs re-election bid?
text: Battle for the ballot: Unlike earlier polls that centred on economic growth, this time the focus is security As he faces his ninth successive Knesset bid on Oct 27, Israeli PM Benjamin Netanyahu is increasingly under scrutiny for his âfailureâ to prevent the Oct 7 massacre. In recent weeks, there has been a broad consensus inside and outside Israel that the Israeli govt, especially its intelligence establishment, failed to act on prior warnings from multiple sources, including Egypt, the UAE, and Palestinians. Arguments about the absence of âactionable intelligenceâ do not hold water, especially with the families who lost their loved ones to incompetence and negligence. While Israel is known for last-minute electoral surprises, the picture is not rosy for Bibi. With more than 19 years in office, Bibi is already Israelâs longest-serving PM and has no intention of hanging up his boots anytime soon. Controversies and scandals are nothing new to him, and they date back to his first prime ministerial bid in May 1996. Unlike other elections in Israel and elsewhere, the forthcoming battle for the ballot does not center on the economy. Despite the war, the economy has recovered from the initial shock, thanks to high-tech resilience. With last weekâs flydubai attempted hijack, the focus is on the proverbial security. There is a political-military divide in Israel over Oct 7. Several senior military and security officials took personal responsibility and left their posts prematurely. This has not been true of the political class. As the ultimate political authority, Netanyahu never took responsibility for the attack and avoided accountability. Initially, he delayed a formal inquiry, citing âongoing warâ, and then he hoped his âvictoryâ would weaken the demand for a judicial postmortem. His high-profile confrontation over controversial judicial reforms also contributed to his refusal. Under Israeli law and norms, a national inquiry commission into major crises is headed by the sitting president of the Israeli Supreme Court, equivalent to the Chief Justice of India. A similar inquiry into the October War of 1973 led to the resignation of PM Golda Meir, and she never returned to active politics. Naturally, Bibi has been averse to such judicial scrutiny. Unfortunately for him, as the Gaza and Iran conflicts dimmed, if not ended, demands for a national inquiry only grew. Indeed, all the major parties and leaders running in the election later this month are pledging a judicial inquiry into the failure. The field is also crowded with several former generals and intelligence figures who strongly disapprove of Bibiâs handling of Oct 7 and its aftermath. Hence, as much as he tries to avoid it, the massacre looms large over the electorate. Mainly due to the proportional system of elections, Israel has not had a single-party govt since 1948. Bibi is unlikely to secure even half of the majority mark. With his popularity falling, the latest opinion polls give Likud party only 18-21 seats, far fewer than the 32 seats it secured in the 2022 election. While he has established complete control over the ruling Likud, Bibi faces severe challenges from the right wing, which opposes even his minimalist accommodation of President Donald Trumpâs Gaza Peace Plan. Otzma Yehudit (led by Itamar Ben-Gvir) and the Religious Zionist Party (headed by Bezalel Smotrich) oppose Bibi on the Gaza Strip and are projected to take a significant share of Likudâs voters. There are other significant contenders. Yashar, led by former general Gadi Eisenkot, is projected to be the largest party, expected to secure 21-25 seats. The rechristened âTogether,â the former Naftali Bennett-Yair Lapid coalition, could be another major player among centrist voters. Above all, the Democrats (the erstwhile Labour-Left coalition) are showing signs of revival and could garner some votes. For a long time, opposition disunity, the shrinking of the Left, and a strong alliance with the religious bloc have marked Bibiâs remarkable staying power. This time, the opposition is near-unanimous in rejecting Netanyahuâs refusal to be held accountable for Oct 7. If current projections hold and Likud loses more seats, Bibiâs post-election coalition-formation manoeuvring will be considerably weakened. Should the religious parties gain more seats, his dependence on the right-religious fringe will only increase. An election forecast is a dangerous gamble in Israel, and the signs are not very favourable for Bibi. Likud is unlikely to be the largest party in the next Knesset, but it could hold on to office with sufficient political concessions to the far right and economic incentives for the religious parties. As Israelis head to the polls just days after the third anniversary of the largest single act of terrorism in Israelâs history, Bibi might even do a political somersault and offer some form of judicial review of his role in the Oct 7 attack. Bibi, the proverbial comeback kid, could still spring a surprise and remain in office beyond Oct 27. Disclaimer : Views expressed above are the author's own.

title: At least 30 arrested, including actors, politicians during anti-Netanyahu protest outside UN
text: Anti-Netanyahu protest outside UN: 30+ arrested, including actors, politiciansUN General Assembly Police arrested at least 30 people, including actors and politicians, during a protest outside the United Nations headquarters on Thursday against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, hours before he addressed the UN General Assembly. Oscar-winning actor Susan Sarandon, Emmy winner Hannah Einbinder, Democratic congressional candidate Darializa Avila Chevalier and New York City Council member Chi Osse were among those arrested, according to Reuters. The protest was organised by Jewish Voice for Peace, a Jewish activist group that supports Palestinians. Around 200 people gathered outside the UN headquarters wearing identical white T-shirts carrying slogans including âFund people not bombs,â âNo warâ and âFree Palestine.â The demonstration came as Netanyahu prepared to address the General Assembly amid international criticism of Israelâs military campaign in Gaza and its broader regional military operations. The protesters blocked traffic outside the UN headquarters, prompting police to order them to leave through loudspeakers. Some demonstrators moved to the sidewalks, but a core group remained seated on the pavement and continued chanting slogans against Netanyahu. Police officers, who arrived on bicycles, surrounded the protesters before beginning arrests. Officers pulled protesters from the group one by one, tied their hands behind their backs with zip ties and escorted them to police buses. The activists continued chanting âNetanyahu go to hellâ outside the buses as arrests continued. Protester says Gaza destruction is being carried out in USâ name Manijeh Moradian, a 50-year-old university professor of Iranian and Jewish heritage who participated in the demonstration, said protesters had a responsibility to speak out against Israelâs actions in Gaza. âWhatâs being done to Gaza, the obliteration of an entire society, in our name, with our tax dollars, this is our responsibility to speak out against, and Netanyahu has no right to use the platform of the United Nations to justify these atrocities,â Moradian said. Inside the General Assembly, Netanyahu defended Israelâs military actions and sought to counter criticism of the country as dozens of delegates walked out of the hall as he began his address. The Israeli prime minister defended Israelâs actions in Gaza and against Iran and other regional adversaries, while also praising US President Donald Trump for his support. Netanyahu's speech came as Israel faced growing international criticism over the humanitarian situation in Gaza and its military campaign across the region. The protest outside the UN and the walkout inside the General Assembly underscored the divisions surrounding Netanyahuâs appearance at the world body. You use AI every day. title: 'No obligations under Rome Statute for overflights': France defends not arresting Netanyahu
text: Benjamin Netanyahu (File photo) France has defended its decision not to arrest Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu despite an International Criminal Court (ICC) warrant against him. Netanyahuâs plane crossed French airspace on Thursday en route to the United Nations. As a signatory to the ICCâs founding Rome Statute, France is formally bound to cooperate with the court, including by arresting suspects who enter its territory. French foreign ministry spokesperson Pascal Confavreux told reporters the clearance to Netanyahu's aircraft was "in full conformity with international law." "The Rome Statute does not impose any obligations regarding overflights of its territory by a state plane which has a passenger who is targeted by an arrest warrant," Confavreux said. According to flight-tracking app Flightradar24, Netanyahuâs plane flew over Greece, Italy and France. An Italian foreign ministry spokesperson said they could not immediately confirm whether Israel had sought permission for the overflight. Netanyahu faces restrictions on travel to several countries because of an ICC arrest warrant issued against him and his former defence minister Yoav Gallant, as well as a separate warrant for a former Hamas military commander, in 2024. Last year, Netanyahu took a circuitous route to New York to avoid the airspace of several European countries, including France, according to media reports. Israel rejects the ICCâs jurisdiction and denies committing war crimes in Gaza. It says its military campaign was aimed at eliminating Hamas following the groupâs October 7, 2023, attack on Israel. Israel is contesting the warrants against Netanyahu and Gallant. The United States, a close Israeli ally and non-signatory to the Rome Statute, has launched a campaign to isolate the court. President Donald Trump this week urged members of The Hague-based court to leave what he called an âout of control institutionâ. France has condemned threats against the ICC. Netanyahu was making a brief visit to the US to address world leaders at the UN General Assembly and was expected to return to Israel later on Thursday. (With Reuters inputs) You use AI every day. title: Palestinian president delivers UN speech by video after US denies visa again
text: Abbas kept from UNGA podium again as US denies visa, speaks by video Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas addressed the UN General Assembly on Thursday through prerecorded remarks from his office in Ramallah after the United States denied visas to him and other senior Palestinian officials to attend the gathering in person for the second consecutive year. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was scheduled to address the assembly in person later on Thursday. Abbas, now 90, has led the Palestinian authority since 2005. The authority is the internationally recognised representative of the Palestinian people, but Abbas's support among Palestinians has declined amid years of criticism over corruption and the sometimes violent expansion of Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank. Under Abbas, Palestine has been recognised as a state by a majority of UN member states. However, those largely symbolic diplomatic gains have not changed Israel's decades-long military occupation of the West Bank. The Palestinian authority has also remained largely sidelined from negotiations over Gaza's future during the ongoing war, with a transition process instead being shepherded by US President Donald Trump's Board of Peace. The Palestinian authority was established under a series of peace agreements with Israel in the 1990s and administers limited self-governing areas of the West Bank. It relies heavily on foreign aid and has not held presidential or legislative elections since 2006. The authority was ousted from Gaza after Hamas won parliamentary elections in 2006 and subsequently seized control of the territory in a violent takeover. Abbas was elected president in 2005 for what was intended to be a four-year term. Israel captured the West Bank and east Jerusalem during the 1967 war. Palestinians seek both territories as part of a future independent state, while Palestinians and much of the international community consider Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank illegal and an obstacle to establishing a viable and contiguous Palestinian state. title: The new Israel-Syria deal: Can US solve the Golan Heights problem?
text: The Golan Heights dispute returned to the centre of the diplomatic spotlight at the United Nations General Assembly in September 2026, when Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa declared that the territory âwill remain Syrianâ, while Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu invoked its biblical links to defend Tel Avivâs claim. Addressing the UN on September 23, al-Sharaa accused Israel of violating Syrian sovereignty through more than 500 air and artillery strikes, over 1,200 land incursions and nearly 300 detentions since the fall of Bashar al-Assad in December 2024. He called for Israeli forces to withdraw to the lines held on December 8, 2024, and reaffirmed Syriaâs commitment to the 1974 disengagement agreement. He also rejected what he described as Israelâs attempt to impose a âfait accompliâ, saying that the Golan would remain Syrian territory. A day later, Netanyahu responded directly to al-Sharaa during his own UN General Assembly address. âMr. al-Sharaa, you should know the Jews have been on the Golan Heights since the days of Moses. You can read it in the Bible,â he said, invoking Israelâs historical and religious links to the plateau. The exchange captured the central challenge facing Washington as it attempts to broker a new security arrangement between the two countries. The US wants to reduce tensions along the Israel-Syria border and create conditions for wider diplomatic engagement. But the disagreement is no longer confined to the Golan Heights, which Israel captured from Syria in 1967 and annexed in 1981. Since Assadâs fall in December 2024, Israeli forces have established positions inside southern Syria, while Damascus has demanded their withdrawal. The violence in the Druze-majority province of Suwayda in July 2025 has added another layer of mistrust, raising questions about whether a border agreement can address Israelâs concerns over the treatment of minorities. Washington may be able to negotiate security zones and monitoring arrangements. Whether it can bridge the two countriesâ competing claims over territory, sovereignty and security is a much harder question. Why the Golan remains a central dispute The Golan Heights is a strategic plateau overlooking northern Israel and southern Syria. Its elevated terrain offers military and surveillance advantages, making it important to Israelâs defence planning. Israel captured the territory from Syria during the 1967 Arab-Israeli war and extended its law and administration to it in 1981. That annexation was rejected by the United Nations and most of the international community. UN Security Council Resolution 497, adopted on December 17, 1981, declared Israelâs decision to impose its laws and administration on the Golan ânull and voidâ and without international legal effect. The UN continues to regard the territory as occupied Syrian land. The strategic plateau overlooks northern Israel and southern Syria, offering commanding views of the border and a military advantage. Its control remains a major point of contention between the two countries. The United States departed from its previous position on March 21, 2019, when then-President Donald Trump announced that Washington would recognise Israeli sovereignty over the Golan. The decision reversed decades of US policy, but did not change the position of the UN or most countries. Colombiaâs recognition of Israelâs claim in August 2026 made it the second country to do so, according to reports. The dispute has endured even during periods when the border remained relatively quiet. Syria has continued to claim the territory, but has not made a serious military attempt to retake it in recent decades. The 1974 disengagement agreement, signed after the 1973 Arab-Israeli war, established a separation zone and restrictions on military deployments, monitored by the United Nations Disengagement Observer Force (UNDOF). That arrangement helped contain direct confrontation, but it did not settle the question of sovereignty. This distinction is central to the current negotiations: a security agreement could regulate military activity without resolving who owns the Golan. What Washington wants from a new agreement The Trump administration is pushing for a security arrangement that could reduce the risk of conflict along the Israel-Syria border. Washington sees such an agreement as a possible first step towards wider diplomatic engagement, including eventual normalisation and Syriaâs entry into the Abraham Accords. The proposed framework, as described in reporting and analysis, would involve a demilitarised zone across southern Syria, a return towards the 1974 disengagement lines, guarantees for the Druze community and an Israeli withdrawal from positions established inside Syrian territory after Assadâs fall. The question of Golan sovereignty would be postponed rather than resolved. The approach reflects a familiar diplomatic calculation: address immediate security concerns first and leave the most politically difficult territorial issue for later. Israel could receive assurances that Syrian forces would not approach the border in strength, while Damascus could maintain that it had not formally surrendered its claim to the Golan. A timeline of the decades-long Israel-Syria dispute, from Israelâs capture of the strategic plateau in 1967 and its 1981 annexation to Donald Trumpâs recognition of Israeli sovereignty in 2019 and the fall of the Assad regime in December 2024. But the two sides disagree over the sequence and terms. Damascus wants Israeli forces to return to the positions they held before December 8, 2024, and says it should retain the right to rebuild its military and determine its alliances. Israel, meanwhile, wants security guarantees and restrictions on military activity in southern Syria before giving up positions it considers valuable. The negotiations have come close to an understanding, but have not produced a durable agreement. Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani said in August 2026 that the two sides had agreed on paper to âalmost everythingâ around the beginning of the year, including arrangements for security zones in southern Syria. But Damascus doubted Israelâs willingness to implement the proposed deal. Why Israel wants military positions inside Syria Israelâs military presence inside Syria expanded after Assad was toppled in December 2024. Israeli forces moved into areas near the Golan and the UN-patrolled buffer zone, while Israel also struck Syrian military facilities and other targets. Israel has described these actions as defensive measures intended to prevent threats from emerging near its border. The positions offer more than a physical buffer. They can provide observation over approaches to the Golan, improve Israelâs ability to monitor movement in southern Syria and give its military more time to respond to potential threats. The terrain around Mount Hermon is particularly important because elevated ground offers a broad view of surrounding territory. The military presence also gives Israel leverage in negotiations. A withdrawal can become part of a broader bargain involving security guarantees, limits on Syrian military deployments and monitoring mechanisms. From Israelâs perspective, leaving without enforceable assurances could mean giving up a strategic advantage while relying on a government whose future conduct remains uncertain. For Damascus, however, the same positions represent an infringement on sovereignty. Syria argues that Israel should withdraw from territory it entered after Assadâs fall before the two sides discuss a longer-term security arrangement. The disagreement was underscored on September 9, 2026, when Netanyahu visited an Israeli military position on Mount Hermon, inside Syrian territory. He said Israel had established âabsolute controlâ over an area stretching from the mountainâs summit south to the Yarmouk River and west to the Mediterranean Sea. Syrian officials condemned the visit as a violation of the countryâs sovereignty and territorial integrity. The RSIS analysis published on September 17, 2026, said a framework under discussion included an Israeli withdrawal from nine outposts established inside the Syrian Golan over the preceding year. These positions have therefore become a test of whether the two sides can translate diplomatic understandings into a change on the ground. The Suwayda crisis: The obstacle beyond the Golan The violence in Suwayda in July 2025 exposed a problem that a border agreement may not be able to solve. The province, in southern Syria, has a large Druze population. A local conflict escalated after government forces entered the area, widening into a crisis involving government troops, tribal fighters and Druze armed groups. A United Nations inquiry later put the death toll above 1,700, most of them Druze civilians, and said that government troops, tribal fighters and Druze militias may have committed war crimes. Israel intervened militarily, striking the Defence Ministry in Damascus and government forces near Suwayda. It said its actions were intended to protect the Druze community. The episode matters because it shaped Israelâs assessment of the new Syrian authorities. If Damascus uses force against a minority community, Israel may see a reason to intervene regardless of what happens along the Golan border. In that scenario, a demilitarised zone could reduce the risk of a conventional military clash but would not prevent a crisis elsewhere in Syria from drawing Israel in. A September 17, 2026, analysis by the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies argued that Washington may be misdiagnosing the central obstacle by focusing too heavily on Golan demilitarisation. Its assessment is that the deeper issue is whether the Syrian government can be trusted not to coerce or attack minority communities. A security agreement could establish rules between two states, but it could not guarantee how Damascus would treat its own citizens. This is also where proposed guarantees for the Druze become difficult. A written commitment may be possible, but enforcing it would require clarity about who monitors violations, what happens if Syrian forces enter the province and whether Israel would retain the right to intervene. Those questions go beyond the technical design of a border arrangement. Al-Sharaaâs position: Security first, Golan later? Al-Sharaa has signalled that Syria is willing to discuss security arrangements, but has resisted any suggestion that Damascus can abandon its claim to the Golan. In April 2026, he indicated that Syria could discuss the Golan at a later stage if Israel withdrew from territory seized after Assadâs fall. His September 23 address at the UN, however, left little doubt that Damascus would not accept a settlement that treated the Golan as territory Washington could allocate. Al-Sharaa invoked Security Council Resolution 497 and called on international partners to abide by it. He also reaffirmed Syriaâs commitment to the 1974 agreement and demanded that Israeli forces withdraw to the lines held on December 8, 2024, the day Assad was removed from power. His position reflects a domestic political constraint. Any Syrian leader who appears to surrender the Golan would face opposition, particularly after years of conflict and foreign intervention. Al-Sharaa has therefore tried to separate the immediate security question from the long-term sovereignty dispute. At an Atlantic Council event on September 22, 2026, he said negotiations with Israel had resolved nearly 90% of the outstanding issues needed for a security agreement. He also joked that he had asked Trump why he did not give Israel New Jersey instead of the Golan. The remarks suggested that Damascus was still open to an agreement, but not to giving up its territorial claim. Netanyahuâs position: Security zones and sovereignty Netanyahuâs UN remarks reinforced Israelâs refusal to relinquish its claim to the Golan. By invoking Jewish presence there since the days of Moses, he placed the dispute within a historical and religious framework, rather than treating it only as a question of military control. Israelâs immediate security position is also tied to its expanded military presence in southern Syria. Defence Minister Israel Katz said in response to al-Sharaa that the Golan under Israeli sovereignty was âan inseparable part of the State of Israel foreverâ. He also said Israel would remain on Mount Hermon and in the security zone as long as it perceived a jihadist threat near its border. The remarks underline the gap between the two governments. Syria wants Israeli forces to withdraw to pre-December 2024 lines and restore the 1974 arrangement. Israel wants to retain strategic positions and security zones until it is satisfied that threats from Syrian territory have been removed. That difference also complicates Washingtonâs role. The US can press Israel to redeploy, but it must also address Israeli concerns about the security environment in southern Syria. At the same time, it cannot expect Damascus to accept an open-ended Israeli military presence as the price of negotiations. The Turkey factor complicates Washingtonâs task The Israel-Syria negotiations are also taking place against the backdrop of growing tension between Israel and Turkey. Ankara is a major regional backer of the new Syrian authorities and has an interest in helping rebuild Syriaâs military and state institutions. Israel, meanwhile, is wary of Turkish military influence near its borders and has opposed the possibility of Turkish forces operating at Syrian bases. The issue came into focus in August 2026, when Israel struck the Abu al-Duhur airbase in northwestern Syria. Israel said the strike was intended to prevent a Turkish military deployment, while Syria and Turkey denied that such a deployment was planned. The episode showed how a bilateral Israel-Syria agreement could be affected by a third countryâs role in Syria. For Washington, this creates a difficult balancing act. It wants to prevent Israeli-Turkish competition from destabilising Syria, while also encouraging Damascus to accept security arrangements that Israel considers necessary. But restrictions on Syriaâs military partnerships could be seen in Damascus as an attempt to limit its sovereignty and dictate its regional relationships. The challenge is therefore larger than drawing a new line on a map. Washington must find a formula that addresses Israelâs concerns without turning southern Syria into a zone where Damascus has limited control over its own security policy. Can Washington solve the Golan problem? Washington can help the two sides reach a practical security agreement. It can mediate a return to the 1974 disengagement framework, negotiate monitoring arrangements, define limits on military deployments and establish channels to prevent incidents from escalating. It can also use diplomatic pressure and incentives to encourage Israeli withdrawal from positions established after December 2024. But the United States cannot make the underlying political dispute disappear. Trumpâs 2019 recognition of Israeli sovereignty over the Golan has narrowed Washingtonâs room to act as a neutral mediator on the territorial question. The UN and most of the international community continue to regard the territory as occupied Syrian land, while Israel considers its control essential to national security. Nor can Washington guarantee that future violence inside Syria will not trigger Israeli intervention. The Suwayda crisis demonstrated that Israelâs security calculations extend beyond the immediate border. If Damascus is accused of targeting minorities, a deal focused only on demilitarisation may prove inadequate. The most realistic outcome may therefore be a limited security arrangement rather than a comprehensive peace agreement. Such a deal could reduce the risk of accidental clashes, establish communication channels and clarify military restrictions. It could also create space for future talks on the Golan. But it would not amount to normalisation, and it would not settle the question of sovereignty. The UN exchange between al-Sharaa and Netanyahu showed how far apart the two sides remain. For Syria, the Golan is a matter of sovereignty and international law. For Israel, it is tied to history, security and the military control of strategic terrain. Washington may be able to negotiate a temporary compromise, but a lasting settlement will depend on whether both governments are willing to accept security guarantees without demanding that the other abandon its core position. title: NYC mayor Zohran Mamdani unveils citywide strategy to combat antisemitism as hate crimes rise 8%
text: NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani announces citywide strategy to combat antisemitism. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has unveiled a citywide strategy to combat antisemitism, including new funding for hate-crime prevention, security at Jewish institutions and programmes focused on Jewish history and culture. The plan includes $6.4 million for the Partners Against the Hate grant programme and $1 million to improve the physical security of synagogues and other houses of worship. The administration will also restart an interagency Security Infrastructure Working Group to help Jewish institutions assess threats and strengthen their security. Mamdani announced the strategy in a two-minute video posted on X on Tuesday, saying he had spent the past year meeting Jewish residents across New York's five boroughs. âAntisemitism is real, and it is growing,â Mamdani said, describing the initiative as âa road map for how our administration will confront the scourge of antisemitismâ. The funding package includes $2 million for the Queens Holocaust Memorial Garden and $2.5 million for the Center for New Jewish Culture in Brooklyn. The administration is also directing money towards hate crime prevention and security initiatives. The announcement comes as antisemitic hate crimes in New York City have risen 8% so far this year, according to NYPD figures released earlier this month. Anti-Jewish incidents account for more than half of all hate incidents recorded in the city. Mamdani has faced criticism from some Jewish organisations over his past comments on Israel and his handling of protests outside synagogues. During his mayoral campaign, his criticism of Israel's conduct during the Gaza war was a prominent part of his platform. He also said during the campaign that, as mayor, he could arrest Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu under an International Criminal Court warrant for alleged war crimes. Mamdani later acknowledged that he would not have the legal authority to make such an arrest. His remarks about the American Israel Public Affairs Committee and its spending in US elections have also drawn criticism. At a rally this summer, Mamdani compared the organisation and its spending to âmonstersâ. Four Jewish organisations, the United Jewish Appeal Federation of New York, Jewish Community Relations Council of New York, American Jewish Committee and New York Board of Rabbis, said the new strategy contained some positive measures but did not address what they considered a key concern. âRhetoric that demonizes and delegitimizes Israel inevitably leads to the targeting of Jewish New Yorkers,â the groups said in a joint statement. Other Jewish leaders welcomed the initiative. Amy Spitalnick, CEO of the Jewish Council for Public Affairs, said the city needed a government-wide response to antisemitism, extremism and violence. âAt a moment of real and rising antisemitism, extremism and violence across the ideological spectrum, our communities deserve a whole-of-government response,â Spitalnick said. New York City Council Speaker Julie Menin also backed the additional funding for security and Holocaust education. Menin previously proposed legislation requiring police to publish plans for establishing buffer zones around schools and houses of worship during protests. âJewish New Yorkers, and everyone in our city, deserve to be safe,â Menin said.
