title: Irish football body launches review over alleged racist âmonkey chantsâ after UEFA refuses to investigate Ireland-Israel clash
text: Players of Israel, right, and Ireland stand for the anthems before the UEFA Nations League soccer match between Ireland and Israel in Debrecen, Hungary, Sunday, Sept. 27, 2026. (Zsolt Czegledi/MTI via AP) The Football Association of Ireland is reviewing footage and audio recordings after an allegation that Irish forward Adam Idah was subjected to racist chanting during Irelandâs 3â0 Nations League win over Israel. The claim emerged after midfielder Jayson Molumby alerted match officials during the game, while UEFA has told the FAI that its own disciplinary process cannot begin because the required reporting procedure was not followed. FAI review allegations after Molumby raises concern during match The allegation centres on events during Irelandâs 3â0 victory over Israel at the Nagyerdei Stadium in Debrecen, Hungary, on Sunday. Idah, who scored Irelandâs second goal, is reported to have been targeted by chants from sections of the Israeli support. The 25-year-old, who was born to a Nigerian father and an Irish mother, was said to be unaware of the alleged abuse while the match was taking place. According to The Irish Times , Molumby heard what he believed were racist chants aimed at Idah before half-time. The Ireland midfielder approached referee Harm Osmers and fourth official Florian Exner and asked them to âlistenâ, pointing towards the stands. X/@Red_united03 | According to FAI, Irish midfielder Jayson Molumby heard chants directed at Adam Idah. The officials did not hear chanting that they considered racist and the incident was not formally reported on the pitch as a racial-abuse allegation. A UEFA match delegate later informed the FAI that the matter could not be investigated through UEFA's disciplinary process because the correct protocol had not been followed. Molumby had not explicitly identified the chanting as racist when speaking to the officials, while the officials themselves had not heard the alleged abuse. The FAI has since decided to conduct its own review. The association is examining available video and audio footage to establish what was said in the stands and whether Idah was subjected to racist abuse. Al Jazeera has reported that videos circulating on social media appear to show Israeli supporters directing âmonkey chantsâ towards Idah during the match. Israeli supporters also filmed military chants after the defeat The allegations surrounding Idah emerged alongside another incident involving supporters in the Israeli section of the stadium. Youseph Haddad, who is described in the reporting as a member of an Israeli right-wing party and a candidate for the country's upcoming parliamentary elections, filmed himself among supporters during the match and posted footage on social media. The video showed supporters chanting about the Israeli military as their team fell to a 3â0 defeat. âYes, we lose in football, but where we donât lose, the IDF [Israeli Defence Force]. We always win,â Haddad said in the video. âSo maybe the football Irish team beat us on the football field, but they will never, ever break the Israeli spirit.â It is not clear whether the chants about the Israeli military would fall within UEFA's rules on spectator behaviour. UEFA's disciplinary regulations allow sanctions ranging from fines to stadium closures and restrictions on away supporters when national associations are found responsible for prohibited spectator conduct, but such penalties require a disciplinary process. The match itself had already attracted significant attention before kick-off because of political pressure surrounding Ireland's decision to fulfil its Nations League fixtures against Israel. The FAI had previously asked UEFA whether Ireland and Israel could be kept apart in future competition draws. UEFA rejected that request, saying such decisions were not based on public sentiment and noting that the countries had never been in direct conflict. Ireland's players had already taken several symbolic actions The events in Debrecen came after days of internal discussions within the Ireland squad over whether the fixture should be played. Goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu withdrew from the squad after speaking with his teammates and explaining that he did not feel he could participate in the matches against Israel. âI am a man of strong faith and try my best to be a person of character and principle. Therefore, I feel it would be wrong to participate in the upcoming fixtures against Israel,â Bazunu said. Ireland ultimately went ahead with the match after discussions between the players and the FAI. The decision came after months of pressure from campaigners calling for the fixtures to be boycotted in response to Israel's war in Gaza. On the pitch, Ireland's players wore black armbands, with FAI chief executive David Courell saying they were worn in recognition of âall lives lostâ in the conflict. The players also bowed their heads during Israel's national anthem and did not shake hands with their opponents before kick-off. Ireland captain Dara O'Shea did not shake hands with Israel captain Dor Peretz, while reports also said O'Shea had pledged to donate his match earnings to humanitarian aid for Gaza. The match itself remained one-sided. Troy Parrott opened the scoring, Idah added the second and Jack Moylan completed the 3â0 victory. Jake O'Brien and Manor Solomon also clashed during the match The political tension surrounding the fixture spilled into an on-field exchange involving Ireland defender Jake O'Brien and Israel winger Manor Solomon. Reports said the two players became involved in an angry confrontation during the match, with O'Brien allegedly telling Solomon: âShame on you for what youâre doing in Gaza. You deserve to lose.â Solomon responded: âCome out, be a man. Donât talk behind a wall. Itâs a shame the game wasnât in Israel, you would understand what the best country in the world is.â Speaking after the match, Solomon declined to repeat what had been said during the confrontation but made clear that the relationship between the two sides had become hostile. âThey said nonsense during the game, I donât want to comment on them,â Solomon said. He further added that he held back from saying more because of the possibility of suspension. âIf I say what I think about them Iâll probably be banned for a few games so I donât want to say, of course they hate us and we donât like them.â Solomon also looked ahead to the return fixture. âIâm already looking forward to the next game against them, itâs going to be completely different.â He later added: âThey (the Irish players) donât interest me. We have a country ten times better than theirs, stronger, an amazing country with amazing people.â âWe are proud to wear the team shirt and to be Israelis. We are proud of our state and of our soldiers.â âThey can play all their tricks. We are Israelis and love the country. And that will always be the case.â Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines Ireland's next Nations League match is against Austria at the Aviva Stadium on October 1, while Israel will host Kosovo on the same day. The return fixture between Ireland and Israel is scheduled for October 4 at the TSC Arena in BaÄka Topola, Serbia. title: 66 projects, $2.45 billion: Trumpâs Board of Peace to unveil six-month Gaza recovery plan, says report
text: Trump said on Tuesday that nearly 30 countries had joined the Board of Peace overseeing Gaza's stabilisation and reconstruction The Board of Peace, set up by US President Donald Trump, will reportedly unveil a six-month, $2.45 billion recovery plan for Gaza on Wednesday, outlining 66 projects focused on rebuilding infrastructure, restoring essential services, reviving the economy and establishing post-war governance. The plan, prepared over the past year by officials from the Board of Peace and the Palestinian technocratic government, includes funding for temporary housing, rubble removal, hospital repairs, economic recovery and the deployment of a multinational security force. But its implementation will depend on cooperation from Israel and Hamas. Israel has agreed in principle to some elements of the proposal but has refused to begin implementing it, while Hamas has agreed in principle to disarm but the process has yet to be tested. The Board of Peace hopes the recovery process can begin after Israel's October 27 election and the formation of a new government. However, the election could result in political deadlock, potentially further delaying the proposal. "The plan shows how to stand up a government from nothing, an economy from shambles and a territory from disaster," a Board of Peace official said. The proposal estimates physical damage in Gaza at $35.2 billion and says full recovery and reconstruction will require about $71.4 billion over the next decade. Infrastructure accounts for the largest share of the six-month plan, at roughly $1 billion. It includes about $400 million for temporary shelters, $275 million for rubble and unexploded ordnance clearance, $50 million for hospital rehabilitation and $30 million for road repairs. The plan also calls for repairing border crossings, restoring electricity and water infrastructure, deploying 25,000 portable solar-power kits and permanently filling tunnels beneath sites needed for priority reconstruction projects. Security-related projects account for roughly $885 million, including $275 million for a permanent site in Rafah capable of supporting 5,000 personnel from the International Stabilization Force and $140 million to recruit, train, equip and deploy a multinational security contingent. Another $120 million would go towards mobilising Palestinian police, while $20 million would fund a weapons buy-back programme offering incentives for Hamas and other armed groups to surrender weapons and ammunition. The plan also allocates about $400 million for insulated caravans for Palestinians currently living in tents. Separately, the UAE would fund a pilot "Emirati Neighborhood" in Rafah designed to house 50,000 people, while about $300 million would go towards health, education and welfare programmes. The proposal also includes a digital ID system, digital payments, 4G connectivity, electronic health and education systems, grants to restart small businesses and a new Gaza investment fund. The Board of Peace and the Palestinian technocratic government say the recovery should be Palestinian-led and based on "Palestinian ownership". The two sides have yet to secure the full $2.45 billion required for the six-month programme, although Board of Peace officials said the entire amount would not be needed immediately. Representatives from 35 countries are expected to attend Wednesday's briefing, including officials from the European Union and several of its member states. title: Security lapse Israel overlooked? Over 12 Omani pilots flew to Tel Aviv despite ban
text: A plane, carrying passengers who were on the FlyDubai aircraft bound for Israel from the United Arab Emirates, which was diverted to Saudi Arabia following an emergency signal. Israeli authorities are facing tough questions over how an Omani pilot was able to fly into Tel Aviv despite a rule barring pilots from countries without diplomatic relations with Israel, according to a report by Channel 12. The issue came to light after a hijacking attempt was made on a flydubai flight on Wednesday when its Omani co-pilot allegedly attacked the captain, Smit Machchhar, and attempted to deliberately crash the aircraft. Israeli passengers, the captain and other pilots on board intervened, allowing the plane to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia. Most of the passengers were Israeli and were later flown from Saudi Arabia to Israel. Over 12 Omani pilots flew into Israel Oman does not have diplomatic relations with Israel. According to the report, rules introduced after the 2020 Abraham Accords prohibit pilots from countries that do not have relations with Israel from flying into the country. However, Channel 12 reported that dozens of Omani pilots had flown into Israel in recent years while working for foreign airlines. The report said Israeli authorities had largely relied on airlines themselves to ensure that pilots from countries without diplomatic ties with Israel did not operate flights into the country. Channel 12 reported that the Shin Bet security service did not independently investigate the nationalities or backgrounds of flydubai pilots. Instead, it had asked the airline not to use pilots from countries that do not have diplomatic relations with Israel. âThe Shin Bet has all the means to know, within five minutes, who all of the pilots on the Dubai airline are, and they simply chose to turn a blind eye,â the network quoted an anonymous airline industry official as saying. âIn Israel, they expected the airline to be reliable enough, so they didnât conduct reviews in recent years.â Israel's Transportation Ministry said the Shin Bet had not issued a specific warning about flydubai, apart from requesting increased baggage checks, according to the report. Security procedures now under scrutiny The incident has prompted authorities to examine how flight crews from foreign airlines are cleared to enter Israel. Channel 12 reported that the Transportation Ministry and its Center for Aviation Security Operations, which was established in recent years to oversee and monitor the entry of flight crews, will be examined as part of the investigation. The State Comptroller's Office had already recommended in 2024 that the government review security procedures related to air travel. The report also pointed to an earlier dispute between the Shin Bet and Israeli airlines El Al, IsraAir and Arkia. In July, the security service barred the three carriers from landing in Dubai because of concerns over regional tensions linked to the war with Iran. Although that decision involved Israeli airlines rather than foreign carriers, Channel 12 reported that applying similarly strict security measures to foreign airlines could potentially have helped prevent Wednesday's incident. Investigation points to possible terror motive Investigations into the attack are continuing in Israel, the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia. The Shin Bet and Mossad are also reportedly cooperating with security agencies in the two countries. Saudi Arabia said the captain and co-pilot, who were treated in hospital for their injuries, left for Abu Dhabi on Thursday after receiving medical clearance. Initial information shared with Israeli authorities reportedly suggested that the co-pilot may have attacked for nationalist reasons, raising the possibility that the incident was treated as a terror attack. The assessment was reportedly based partly on statements the co-pilot made to Saudi investigators, along with other information gathered during the probe. Israeli PM Benjamin Netanyahu said earlier Thursday that the Omani first officer âunderwent Islamist radical indoctrination.â Channel 12 said that assessment was based on information from two Israeli sources familiar with the Saudi investigation. The motive has not been independently established, and investigations by authorities in the three countries remain ongoing. You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

title: 20 dead, dozens missing after war-damaged apartment block collapses in Gaza
text: Civil Defence workers attempt to rescue people trapped beneath the rubble of a residential building that had been damaged in an earlier Israeli strike during the war and collapsed on Wednesday, in Gaza City. Gaza rescuers on Wednesday searched through the wreckage of a bomb-damaged apartment building that collapsed overnight in Gaza City. The incident killed at least 20 Palestinians, including five children, and left nearly 100 people feared trapped under the rubble. The seven-storey building collapsed in the Tal al-Hawa area, where at least 10 families were living. Fourteen people were injured in the collapse, while rescue workers continued searching for survivors. Watch Muslim Nations WARN Netanyahu: Palestinians Cannot Be Removed From Gaza Under Any Label Raed Al-Dahshan, director of Gaza City's civil defence service, said rescuers could still hear people beneath the debris. "We are still hearing voices from under the rubble, so there is still hope to find people," said Dahshan. Video obtained by Reuters showed rescue workers trying to pull two people from beneath a collapsed wall. Another video circulating on social media showed Gaza civil defence spokesperson Mahmoud Basal carrying a young girl wrapped in a blood-stained scarf. Rescue efforts have been slowed by a lack of heavy machinery and other equipment needed to clear the rubble safely. Residents have also joined civil defence teams in digging through the debris by hand. Alessandro Mrakic, head of the UN Development Programme's Gaza office, said rescuers from some UN agencies were involved in the operation, along with Egypt's relief agency. "The situation, as you see, is tragic because we don't have the equipment and machinery that is needed. So there are actually people that are digging with their bare hands. We need to prepare (for more deaths)," said Mrakic. Mrakic said hundreds of other buildings were also at risk. "There are approximately 400 buildings at risk of collapse. And we know that these buildings will collapse, especially now with the upcoming winter," he added. The collapse has highlighted the dangers facing thousands of Palestinians who have moved into damaged buildings because of a severe shortage of shelters and tents. Gaza's local rescue service estimates that about 2,000 damaged buildings are still inhabited by families. Dahshan said at least 10 families had been living in the collapsed building and warned residents against entering damaged structures. "The limited availability of shelter options forced residents to move into this building, believing it was safe. However, at one point it collapsed entirely, tragically crashing down on people as they slept," said Dahshan. Many families have told Reuters in recent months that they were living in partially damaged buildings to protect themselves from wind and rain. The shortage of new tents has also left many people with few alternatives. Palestinian and UN officials have blamed Israeli restrictions on the entry of heavy machinery for the difficulties faced by rescue teams. Israel says the restrictions are intended to prevent such equipment from reaching militant groups. The building collapse is also part of a wider problem across Gaza, where thousands of structures have been damaged or partially destroyed during the war. The UN estimates that Israel's assault on Gaza, launched after Hamas' deadly attack on Israel in October 2023, has generated around 61 million tonnes of rubble and debris. It could take seven years to clear it. An October 2025 US-backed ceasefire halted large-scale fighting in Gaza, but Israeli strikes have continued and negotiations over a lasting peace have made little progress. Hamas has accused Israel of violating the ceasefire and obstructing US President Donald Trump's broader plan to end the conflict. The plan includes an Israeli withdrawal from Gaza and the disarmament of Hamas. Israel, meanwhile, has accused Hamas of violating the agreement. title: 'NAZA': Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor's Gaza documentary to stream for free after global release
text: Gaza documentary 'NAZA' to stream for free post global release 'NAZA', the documentary about the killings in Gaza, by Israeli filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szo, will be available to watch for free after its global release, reported Variety. The documentary won a special jury prize at the recently concluded Venice Film Festival. According to Variety, the documentary will be made visible to global audiences for free via the website of British newspaper The Guardian after its release in theatres worldwide on September 28, following its world premiere at Venice. It will be available to watch for free in late November. "NAZA shows in detail the systems behind Israel's calculated mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza," according to its official synopsis. The documentary was shot in secrecy at night on the rooftops of Tel Aviv and features revelatory interviews with 24 Israeli military intelligence officers and soldiers. 'NAZA,' a term that appears throughout the documentary, is an acronym for collateral damage used by Israeli intelligence to indicate the number of civilians it expects will be killed in an airstrike. 'NAZA' director Yuval Abraham also announced the documentary's free worldwide streaming on his X handle, saying the decision was prompted by the "interest and public importance" of the documentary. He wrote, "Due to the interest and public importance, I and Rachel decided together with The Guardian that the film NZA would be accessible online for free, without any time limit, so that every person can watch it and the soldiers' testimonies. This will happen in a few weeks, in November, at the earliest date we managed to set. Until then, we approached cinemas in Israel and offered them the film at no cost, in the hope that it will be screened in the country already now, in parallel to its distribution in cinemas around the world. Its screening will be a brave decision in the face of great violence aimed at concealing it. I know there is enormous demand to watch the film, and I hope that in this way, everyone will soon be able to see it: whether in cinemas or online in a few weeks." Abraham and Szor were two of the four directors of 'No Other Land,' which won the 2025 Best Documentary Oscar and depicts the Israeli government's efforts to force Palestinians from their homes in the southern West Bank. Kraft, who is Jewish, accused the rapper of hate speech and said he was âonly sharing selective information and ignoring the actions of Hamasâ. Despite the controversy, several fans attending Sheeranâs Philadelphia concert said they continued to support the singer. title: Did Israel ignore warnings? UAE shared info about flydubai crew & Omani co-pilot before flight
text: Oman had barred al-Hammami from flying because of concerns that he had adopted extremist views The United Arab Emirates had shared with Israel information on the passengers and crew aboard the FlyDubai flight whose Omani co-pilot allegedly attacked the captain and tried to seize control of the aircraft, according to regional officials cited by The Associated Press. The disclosure has raised fresh questions over how the co-pilot was able to board an Israel-bound flight despite having previously been barred from flying by Oman over concerns about his extremist views. The UAE, which is leading the investigation, has described Wednesday's incident as a âterrorist attackâ. The co-pilot allegedly attacked Captain Smit Machchhar with the cockpit's crash axe before attempting to take control of the plunging aircraft. The plane, carrying 182 people, was eventually stabilised after the injured captain managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers and others to overpower the attacker. Also read: Crew of flydubai demanded release of co-pilot after he attacked Smit, claim flyers The latest details have put the spotlight on possible security failures in Israel, the UAE and the airlines involved. According to regional officials cited by AP, the UAE had provided Israel with information about those aboard the flight, including their nationalities. Israel, however, had not raised any red flags over either a passenger or crew member, the officials said. Israel's security system under scrutiny The Shin Bet, Israel's domestic security agency, has said responsibility for vetting passenger lists from foreign flights lies with the transportation ministry. Transportation minister Miri Regev, however, told public broadcaster Kan that security agencies were responsible for flight security and that her ministry had not been given a passenger list or any warning about the co-pilot. Also read: Co-pilot's chilling admission after trying to crash flydubai jet The Times of Israel, citing Army Radio and internal National Security Council documents, reported that Israeli security bodies had warned for years that the Transportation Ministry was not adequately equipped to carry out security checks on foreign airlines flying into the country. In 2021, Israel's security cabinet removed responsibility for such checks from the Shin Bet and assigned the Civil Aviation Authority, under the transportation ministry, responsibility for ensuring that security procedures on foreign flights met international requirements. A classified 2024 state comptroller report reportedly found that the ministry was not meeting its obligations. In May 2024, the security cabinet ordered the National Security Council to form a team involving the Transportation Ministry, Civil Aviation Authority, Shin Bet, Mossad and Finance Ministry to examine the security framework for international commercial flights. On September 30, flydubai Flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv experienced an in-flight cockpit attack. The discussions continued for about a year. According to documents cited by Army Radio, the Shin Bet said it lacked the manpower and budget to handle security checks for foreign flights, while the NSC agreed that the Transportation Ministry should assume responsibility but said it would need additional resources. There was reportedly strong internal opposition within the ministry. One source involved in the discussions told Army Radio: âThe Shin Bet and Mossad knew full well that the Transportation Ministry was in pieces, that it had no people, no positions, and no capabilities.â The source added: âHow did they just shrug off responsibility like that and dump everything on the transportation ministry? The responsibility lies with the transportation ministry â but the Shin Bet and Mossad also enabled this failure, and the writing was on the wall.â The transportation ministry has rejected the allegations as âcompletely falseâ. It said responsibility for foreign flights had existed within the ministry for decades and that it was incorrect to portray it as a recently transferred responsibility. It also said the National Security Council and other security bodies had approved its procedures. Co-pilot was previously barred from flying The scrutiny is particularly sharp because the co-pilot, identified by people familiar with the investigation as Hamam al-Hammami, had reportedly already come to the attention of authorities in Oman. According to AP, a regional official and another person familiar with the matter said Oman had barred al-Hammami from flying because of concerns that he had adopted extremist views. He was subsequently moved to an administrative position at Oman Air before later being hired by UAE-based FlyDubai. A Gulf diplomat cited by AP said al-Hammami had undergone standard security checks before being hired, but those checks appeared to focus on criminal convictions rather than examining his background for possible signs of radicalisation. The incident has also raised questions over how an Omani national was permitted to serve on a flight carrying Israeli passengers. Israel and Oman do not have diplomatic relations, and Israel has said it has agreements with foreign airlines restricting pilots from countries without diplomatic ties from operating flights to the country. The UAE has shared information about the incident with Israel as the investigation continues. Four regional countries are reportedly working to establish the co-pilot's motive, with assistance from the US and other Western governments. Investigators have so far not found a connection between him and a militant group, according to a Gulf diplomat cited by AP. You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

text: Some âfriendsâ are far worse than enemies, and you can put terrorists at the top of that list. Consider Osama bin Laden . title: âWake upâ: Iran releases 25-page letter urging US voters to reject Trump ahead of midterms
text: The letter was released about five weeks before the US midterm elections Iranâs Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has made a direct appeal to American voters, urging them to reject President Donald Trump âs policies and âwrest control back from corrupt politiciansâ as the US heads towards its midterm elections. In a lengthy open letter addressed to the American public, the powerful Iranian military force argued that Washingtonâs war against Iran had failed to achieve its objectives and called for a change in US policy towards Tehran. The 25-page letter, released seven months after the US-Israel war against Iran began, seeks to draw a distinction between the American people and their government. The IRGC argues that ordinary Iranians and Americans share common interests and grievances, portraying both as victims of political leaders pursuing costly wars. It also urges Americans to oppose US support for Israel and foreign military interventions, while presenting peaceful coexistence between Washington and Tehran as possible if US policy changes. IRGC spokesman Gen Hossein Mohebbi reinforced the message at a news conference in Tehran on Tuesday, saying the only way for the conflict to end was for Washington to acknowledge defeat and withdraw. He urged Americans to reconsider their leadership and put pressure on the Trump administration, arguing that many US citizens remained unaware of what he described as the âharmsâ caused by its policies. Watch Trump Under Pressure From Veterans & Republican At Home As Iran War Drives Fuel Prices Higher The timing of the letter is significant. The letter was released about five weeks before the US midterm elections, with the IRGC describing the current period as a moment when the American political system is at its weakest. Mohebbi said he did not necessarily expect the letter to change the US administrationâs behaviour, but hoped American voters would hear its message. âWake upâ: Iran takes message to US voters The letter repeatedly attacks Trumpâs justification for the war, particularly his claim that Iranâs nuclear programme posed a threat that required military action. Tehran has consistently denied seeking nuclear weapons and maintains that its uranium enrichment programme has civilian purposes. âThe enemy [US] knows that Iran is not after nuclear weapons,â Mohebbi said, echoing the letterâs argument that Washington has used the nuclear issue as a pretext to pursue wider strategic and economic goals. The IRGC also claims that the US and Israel failed to achieve their stated objectives in the war. According to the letter, the targets shifted repeatedly after earlier goals, including regime change and partition of Iran, were not achieved. It lists objectives ranging from forcing Iranâs unconditional surrender and destroying its nuclear and missile programmes to taking control of the Strait of Hormuz. The letter declares Iran the victor, claiming that thousands of US and Israeli strikes damaged Iranian infrastructure but failed to accomplish their stated aims. It further claims that Iranian forces inflicted major losses on US military assets and severely damaged American bases across the region. These assertions are presented by the IRGC as evidence of a broader strategic defeat for Washington. The Strait of Hormuz features prominently in the letter and Mohebbiâs remarks. He rejected US claims that Iran had lost its leverage over the vital waterway, arguing that the movement of a limited number of vessels did not mean the strait was fully open. Oil exports through the waterway, however, have recovered substantially from the levels seen earlier in the conflict, according to figures cited in the supplied material. âDeath to Americaâ explained as attack on rulers The IRGC letter also attempts to explain one of the most recognisable slogans associated with Iranâs political system: âDeath to Americaâ. It argues that the phrase is directed at the US political establishment rather than the American population. ââDeath to Americaâ is a prayer for the eradication of the diabolical ruling elite whose seat of power is the White House,â the letter says. The document repeatedly contrasts the American public with Washingtonâs political leadership, claiming that taxpayers ultimately bear the financial burden of US wars. It asks Americans to question why their government continues to pursue military confrontation and warns of what it describes as the consequences of an ongoing conflict. The IRGCâs approach echoes Cold War-era efforts to reach an adversaryâs population directly. During the Vietnam War, Vietnamese broadcaster Trinh Thi Ngo, widely known as âHanoi Hannahâ, used English-language broadcasts to target American troops, urging them to question their government and the war. Her programmes highlighted US casualties, anti-war protests and reports critical of the conflict while presenting the Vietnamese sideâs narrative. Iran has similarly sought to communicate directly with Western audiences since the latest war began, using Iran-linked media and online networks, including English-language AI-generated videos, memes and short-form content. The IRGC letter now represents a much more formal version of that strategy: an attempt to speak past Washington and directly to American voters. For Tehran, the central message is that the war is not simply a military confrontation between two states, but a political choice that Americans themselves can challenge. Mohebbi urged them to put pressure on their government, while the letter concluded with a broader argument that Iranâs resistance had demonstrated the limits of American military power. Meanwhile, Iranâs economic pressures remain severe. The rial fell to a new record low on Tuesday, with traders in Tehran reportedly exchanging more than 2.5 million rials for one US dollar. title: Ireland name defender as goalkeeper in bizarre move ahead of reluctant Nations League clash with Israel
text: Ireland's players pose for the team picture before the UEFA Nations League soccer match between Kosovo and Ireland in Pristina, Kosovo, Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026. (AP Photo/Visar Kryeziu) Ireland have found themselves in a remarkably unusual situation ahead of their Nations League meeting with Israel, with QPR defender Jimmy Dunne being listed as a goalkeeper after Gavin Bazunu withdrew from the squad. Bazunu's decision came after a day of lengthy discussions within the Ireland camp over whether the fixture should go ahead at all. The team eventually voted by a âsignificant majorityâ to play, but Bazunu decided he could not take part, saying his personal beliefs meant he felt it would be wrong to participate in the matches against Israel. That left Ireland needing another goalkeeper on the squad list, and Dunne, who normally plays at centre-back for QPR, was the rather unexpected solution. UEFA's squad listing now includes him alongside CaoimhÃ­n Kelleher and Max O'Leary Bazunu pulls out after players spend hours discussing the fixture The Ireland camp had already been under considerable pressure in the build-up to the match, with calls in Ireland for the team to boycott the two Nations League fixtures against Israel. The first meeting is being played in Debrecen, Hungary, with Ireland's other fixture against Israel scheduled for October 4 in BaÄka Topola, Serbia. The controversy surrounding the games has been linked to Israel's military actions in Gaza and the wider political debate around whether Israel should be taking part in international football. Things became particularly tense on Saturday when Ireland's scheduled training session and press conference were delayed by more than five hours while the players discussed whether they should fulfil the fixture. FAI chief executive David Courell said one player had told manager Heimir HallgrÃ­msson that they were uncomfortable taking part and intended to withdraw from the squad. âWhat proceeded was another four hours of conversations, predominantly amongst the players themselves, but also at times with the coaching staff and the executive,â Courell said. âUltimately we carried out a vote amongst the squad ... and it was a significant majority that was returned with the intention to continue.â The player was later confirmed as Bazunu, who explained his decision in a statement posted on Instagram. âRepresenting my country means everything to me. I have the utmost respect for every single one of my teammates, the manager, his staff, and the Irish people,â Bazunu said. âHowever, I have reached a decision that I have not taken lightly. I am a man of strong faith, and try my best to be a person of character and principle, therefore I feel it would be wrong to participate in the upcoming fixtures against Israel.â Bazunu said his decision was based on his personal belief that killing innocent people was wrong, while making clear that he did not intend his position to be directed at Israeli people or the Jewish community. âMy decision is based purely on my personal belief that the killing of innocent people is wrong,â he said. âIt is important to note that my stance is not in opposition of the Israeli people or the Jewish community, but against the atrocities in the region.â He added: âThere are a few times where you get a chance in life to stand up for something bigger, and I strongly believe that this is one of them.â So Ireland turned a defender into a goalkeeper Bazunu's withdrawal left Ireland needing to make a change to their squad, with UEFA regulations requiring three goalkeepers to be listed. The QPR defender is normally used at centre-back and has no regular role as a goalkeeper, but he has now been listed as Ireland's third goalkeeper for the match. UEFA's official squad list places Dunne at No.23 alongside Kelleher and O'Leary. It is an unusual sight for an international squad, but it gives Ireland the third goalkeeper required for the fixture after Bazunu's departure. Courell also confirmed that the players who remain with the squad had agreed to make several changes to the usual matchday routine as a way of showing their unease with the situation. Ireland intend to wear black armbands âin recognition of all the lives lost in the conflictâ, while players will also refrain from parts of the normal pre-match ceremony, including the handshake and exchange of pennants. The squad have also decided to effectively remove their media obligations for the remainder of the international window, according to Courell. The FAI said there would also be significant charitable contributions connected to match fees and revenue from the Austria fixture. title: Netanyahu secretly visited UAE, met Emirati leader in Abu Dhabi: Israeli official
text: Netanyahu's visit comes amid claims that the UAE had warned him shortly before October 7. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu met UAE President Sheikh Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan in Abu Dhabi on Sunday, a senior Israeli official told news agency Reuters, as the two countries navigate a sensitive regional security environment. However, neither Netanyahuâs office nor the UAE foreign ministry immediately issued a public statement on the meeting. The visit comes amid renewed attention in Israel to claims that the UAE leader had warned Netanyahu shortly before Hamasâ October 7, 2023 attack that the group was preparing a major operation. Dispute over reported warning Israeli newspaper Haaretz reported earlier this month that Sheikh Mohammed had raised the warning with Netanyahu around a week and a half before the Hamas attack. The report said the information was not subsequently passed to Israeli intelligence agencies or the military. The issue has become politically sensitive as Netanyahu faces a difficult reelection campaign, with opposition figures accusing him of responsibility for security failures before the October 7 attack. The UAE has not commented directly on the Haaretz report. It has previously said that the two countries have maintained "open and direct lines of communication" since establishing diplomatic relations in 2020. A UAE source previously told Reuters that security issues are discussed with other countries through the "relevant entities", rather than "at the level of national leaders." UAE-Israel ties under scrutiny Earlier this year, the UAE denied that Sheikh Mohammed had met Netanyahu after the Israeli prime minister's office said in May that Netanyahu had "secretly visited" the Gulf country. A person familiar with the meeting later said the two leaders had met in Al-Ain, an oasis city in Abu Dhabi near the border with Oman, on March 26. title: Watch: Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa caught scrolling Instagram Reels during Erdoganâs UN speech
text: Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa was caught on camera scrolling through Instagram Reels at UN meet. Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa was caught on camera scrolling through Instagram Reels on his smartphone as Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan addressed world leaders at the United Nations General Assembly in New York. A video from inside the UNGA hall shows al-Sharaa looking down at his phone and appearing to scroll through Instagram's short-video feed while Erdogan was speaking from the podium. The clip has since gone viral on social media. Some reports said al-Sharaa was also sharing Reels, but the footage itself does not establish what he was watching or whether he was messaging anyone. The moment came as nearly 130 heads of state and government gathered in New York for the 81st UN General Assembly's high-level debate. Erdogan addressed the gathering on Tuesday, speaking about issues including Gaza, Palestinian statehood and reforms to the UN Security Council. Al-Sharaa's second UNGA appearance The viral moment came ahead of al-Sharaa's own appearance at the UN. His visit marks his second attendance at the General Assembly after he became the first Syrian representative in nearly six decades to address world leaders at the UNGA in 2025. Al-Sharaa became Syria's interim president in January 2025 after leading the offensive that overthrew longtime president Bashar al-Assad. Since then, his administration has sought to rebuild Syria's international ties and engage with Western and Arab governments. Al-Sharaa's phone moment contrasted with the major diplomatic issues surrounding his appearance in New York. Syria's new leadership has been seeking international engagement as the country attempts to recover from years of war and political upheaval. Al-Sharaa has also been involved in discussions concerning Syria's relations with Israel and the status of the Golan Heights. title: Iran's 'village' is cracking. How Tehran is keeping its Axis of Resistance alive
text: How and why is Iran keeping its Axis of Resistance alive (AI-generated Image) Mothers and the Islamic Republic of Iran have something unexpected in common: they both understand that it takes a village to raise a child, though what a child and a village mean to each of them differs. For Iran, the child is its influence in the Middle East and its village, the network it has built over the years in this same region ââ Hezbollah in Lebanon, militias in Iraq, the Houthis in Yemen and armed groups elsewhere, each with its own capabilities, interests and relationship with Tehran. The groups operate in very different political and military environments, but together they give Iran a way to contest its adversaries without committing its own forces to every battlefield. But the village is not as strong as it once was, and the recent conflict has shown where its foundations have cracked or given way. How Tehran keeps it standing comes down to four moves: pacing its partners, replacing the ones it has lost, paying for all of it through channels that sanctions have made costlier without closing, and tolerating allies it cannot command. Iran's village The Axis of Resistance exists because of fear. On January 29, 2002, George W Bush put Iran, Iraq and North Korea in his "Axis of Evil", at a moment when the United States had already invaded Afghanistan and was preparing for war in Iraq. American power was closing in on Iran from two sides, and Tehran had reason to believe it could be next. The habit of reaching beyond its borders was by then two decades old. Iran had sent Revolutionary Guards to Lebanon in 1982 to train the Shia fighters who would form Hezbollah, and during the Iran-Iraq war it had organised Iraqi Shia exiles into the force that became the Badr Organization. The speech and the wars that followed turned that habit into a doctrine of strategic depth, in which armed partners in different theatres would force Iran's opponents to account for several fronts at once and keep a confrontation from reaching Iranian territory first. The network was never uniform. Hezbollah became deeply integrated with Tehran, Iraqi militias developed their own political bases, and the Houthis kept far greater autonomy. That unevenness decides what Tehran can ask of each member. The strain Since the war began on 28 February, the arrangement has been tested harder than at any point in its history. Hezbollah has been badly weakened, Syria's role as the land bridge to Lebanon ended with the fall of Assad, and Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei has been killed. A ceasefire and a memorandum of understanding followed in June, then came apart over the Strait of Hormuz. Manish Rai, a geopolitical analyst specialising in the Middle East and Af-Pak region, traces the breakdown to one clause. "The strikes were resumed because of the different interpretations of article 5 in MoU which concerns the Strait of Hormuz," he says. Washington wants the strait kept as it was before 28 February, while Iran, which had begun fining vessels for transiting it, wants control. American forces began nightly strikes on 11 July, and diplomacy has since stalled: by the war's seventh month Trump had rejected an Iranian offer of a seven-day ceasefire, and the Wall Street Journal reported that he expects the bombing to resume after the November midterms. Pace the partners Rai also points out that Tehran has not been to throw everything into the fight at once. To maintain their control the leadership, he says, advised its partners to pursue low-intensity conflict, since an all-out war could destroy groups such as Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad while a slower campaign still drains an adversary. Some groups were held back, among them Bahrain's Al-Ashtar Brigade and the Shia units of Pakistan and Afghanistan, which have gone into what he calls "a bit of hibernation" because Tehran has no wish to open fronts against Islamabad or Kabul. The logic behind their strategy is endurance. Tehran does not need every partner to fight at full strength, or even to enter the war at the same time. It needs enough of them to remain intact, armed and capable of being activated when circumstances demand it. A slower, uneven campaign allows Iran to keep pressure on its adversaries while limiting the risk of exhausting the very groups it may need in a later phase. In that sense, the network is not built for one decisive battle; it is built to absorb losses, preserve its remaining capabilities and keep multiple fronts available for as long as the conflict lasts. Replace what has been lost Hezbollah is the most capable member of the Axis, and Rai argues that if Israel reduces it to a shadow of its former self, the resulting void "cannot be filled by any other Iranian-supported organisations". Diplomacy is working against it as well as force. A US-brokered framework signed on 26 June ties a phased Israeli withdrawal from southern Lebanon to the disarmament of non-state armed groups, a reference to Hezbollah, which rejected the terms and insists that withdrawal come first. That dispute over sequencing has outlasted several rounds of talks, while Israeli strikes in the south continue. File photo: Hezbollah flags flutter as protesters rally to show support to Palestinians in the Gaza Strip and Lebanon's Hezbollah What Tehran can do is shift weight to the partners it still reaches. Iraq's Popular Mobilisation Forces are the obvious candidate, because they are next door and large, an estimated 100,000 to 125,000 fighters by Rai's count, with Kataib Hezbollah and the Badr Organization among them. He describes them as Tehran's "personal favourites", available as ground forces for the Revolutionary Guards and as an internal-security backstop that would free elite Iranian units for operations against the United States and Israel. Substitution also has a limit, Hezbollah has built loyalty over decades through its social services, and as Rai suggests, "if the US, Israel, and international organisations such as the United Nations provide sufficient funding for these services, public support could gradually shift from Hezbollah to the Lebanese state." An army can be replaced faster than a constituency, and that is as true in Beirut as in Tehran's calculations. Keep the money moving All of this has to be paid for, but Iran's financial support for its partners does not move through one pipeline. It runs through a mix of sanctioned oil sales, front companies, informal banking networks, cash, trade intermediaries and, increasingly, digital assets. The system is designed less to make money invisible than to make it difficult for any single disruption to stop the flow altogether. American sanctions this year have targeted several parts of that machinery. In April, Washington moved against an oil-for-gold network that it said generated revenue for Hezbollah and the Quds Force. In July, the US Treasury targeted a maritime-services network linked to Iran that it said used digital assets to facilitate payments, while continuing to sanction vessels involved in the country's shadow-fleet trade. Earlier sanctions have also identified front companies and intermediaries operating outside Iran, including in Hong Kong and the Gulf. Rai describes a parallel informal system in which sanctioned crude is sold through shadow tankers, proceeds are moved through front companies and intermediaries, and hawala networks settle payments across borders without relying on conventional banks. Some money can move as cash, while other transfers can be disguised through commercial transactions, charities or businesses that have legitimate operations alongside their financial role. Cryptocurrency provides another route where conventional banking channels are difficult or unavailable. But the financial relationship between Tehran and its partners is not simply one-way. Hezbollah, the Houthis and other groups have developed their own revenue streams, from businesses and investments to taxation, smuggling and other illicit activity, reducing their dependence on Iranian transfers. That distinction matters because sanctions can make Iranian support more expensive and complicated without necessarily making the organisations themselves financially helpless. The result is a system that is under pressure but difficult to shut down. Every new sanctions round can force Tehran and its partners to change intermediaries, routes or payment methods, but the network has accumulated enough alternative channels to keep at least some money moving. For Iran, financial resilience is therefore less about maintaining an uninterrupted flow than about ensuring that when one channel closes, another remains available. Tolerate allies it cannot command The Houthis show where this strategy runs out. Ansar Allah began in the early 1990s as a nationalist and cultural movement against Salafi influence and the marginalisation of Yemen's Zaydis, and drew close to Tehran only after turning sectarian. It does not accept velayat-e faqih, the doctrine of clerical guardianship that Hezbollah and many Iraqi militias follow, and its first aim is power at home. Rai calls it "an independent ally, rather than a strict proxy". A decade of war has transformed the Houthis from a local insurgency into a force capable of threatening Saudi Arabia, Israel and international shipping The summer tested that, the Houthis stayed out of the Saudi front until 13 July, when Saudi Arabia struck Sanaa airport to stop an Iranian plane returning their delegation from Khamenei's funeral. They responded with missiles at a southern Saudi airport, then declared a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia and hit two major Saudi oil facilities on the Red Sea, and on 8 September a barrage wounded seventy-three people in the kingdom. The Houthis escalated only after an affront to their own delegation, which suits a cautious, self-interested actor, yet their targets are the ones that most relieve pressure on Iran, and Rai says Tehran has encouraged threats against Bab el-Mandeb and the East-West "Petroline" pipeline built to bypass Hormuz. Yemen's war has its own logic too, since government forces say their offensive aims at retaking Sanaa. Tehran can decide when to activate an ally and cannot necessarily dictate how it fights, which is the cost of an Axis that keeps going partly because its members do not wait for orders. Iran gains from Saudi Arabia's predicament, since Riyadh has avoided direct retaliation against Iran, calling the war "not our war", and has refused the US Navy the use of its bases for the Hormuz navigation effort. Rai says it fears offending religious sentiment at home and forfeiting its standing as leader of the Sunni world, while the United Arab Emirates has taken a harder line by cooperating with Israel and striking inside Iran. A divided Gulf suits a strategy of attrition, though Houthi and Iraqi pressure may be pushing Riyadh towards limited retaliation. The test in Iraq Iraq is where the four moves now face their clearest test. On September 30, the United States completed its military withdrawal from Iraq, formally ending the Operation Inherent Resolve mission after more than a decade. Washington will continue to support Baghdad with training and intelligence, but the security responsibility now rests with the Iraqi state. File photo: Members of Iraq's Iran-allied Popular Mobilization Forces carry a portrait of Iran's late Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei as they ride over a US flag during a procession The other deadline did not end with the American departure. Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi had originally tied the disarmament of armed factions to September 30, but Baghdad has since pushed the deadline to June 30, 2027. Under the revised plan, Iran-aligned armed groups are expected to observe a 90-day halt to attacks before beginning a gradual handover of weapons to the state. The timetable is already facing resistance: some of the most powerful factions have rejected the idea of surrendering their weapons voluntarily. That makes the American withdrawal less a conclusion than the beginning of a new test. For years, the presence of US forces gave Iran-backed groups both a target and a justification for maintaining an armed role. With those forces gone, Baghdad has less room to argue that the militias are needed to resist a foreign military presence, but it also has to prove that the state can enforce its authority without triggering a confrontation with the factions themselves. If Baghdad succeeds, Iran's village loses one of its most important advantages: an armed network embedded inside a partner state. If it fails, the American withdrawal may leave the militias with greater room to operate, even as Baghdad formally insists that all weapons must come under state authority. The village has survived by bending: it has paced its partners, shifted weight to those closest to home, found money through channels that pressure has narrowed without closing, and put up with allies who answer to their own politics. The same flexibility that has kept it standing is also what Tehran can no longer fully control. You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump also warned that Iran would be hit âvery hardâ if Tehran was linked to the alleged attempt. Investigation to examine whether the incident was a deliberate attempt to bring down the Israel-bound plane is under way. The aircraft, a Boeing 737 Max 8 carrying 182 people, mostly Israelis, from the United Arab Emirates to Tel Aviv, made an emergency landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, after the co-pilot allegedly stabbed the captain and caused the plane to plunge thousands of feet. Saudi authorities had been conducting the preliminary probe before handing the suspect to the UAE. Israeli intelligence and security officials are also in Saudi Arabia assisting the investigation, while Israel has requested that the co-pilot be sent to Israel for questioning. Investigators examine possible motives The UAE has now taken over the investigation. The Emirati government said its team was examining the attack and âwhether it was linked to any terrorist purposeâ. The UAE has jurisdiction because the aircraft is registered there and its laws apply to crimes committed on board. A regional official said several possibilities remained under investigation, including terrorism and mental disorders. âAll possible scenarios, from terrorism to mental disorders, are being looked into. Nothing is ruled out for now,â the official said. The co-pilot has not been publicly identified. Saudi authorities have been working with countries including Israel to establish a motive, with the UAE, the United States and Oman also involved in the investigation. Israeli officials were in Saudi Arabia to help investigate the suspect, and Israel has requested that he be sent to the country for questioning, although it remains unclear whether the request will be granted. The UAE said its investigation would also examine whether the attack was linked to any terrorist purpose. Israel says co-pilot underwent Islamist indoctrination Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the initial investigation suggested the co-pilot had undergone Islamist indoctrination and may have been trying to crash the aircraft. âThe attacker, the co-pilot who attacked the captain, is now being interrogated. What we know so far is that he underwent Islamist radical indoctrination,â Netanyahu told Fox News. Netanyahu also described the struggle inside the cockpit, saying the co-pilot repeatedly called on crew members to kill him. âThey had to use earphone cords to tie his hands and then used plastic cuffs. He is lying on the floor and he calls out to the crew 'kill me, kill me'. So, it is clear that he was suicidal and was going to down the plane,â he said. An Israeli official separately told The Times of Israel that social media material attributed to the co-pilot included posts about killing Jewish people. The official said the material indicated that he had been radicalised into jihadist ideology, while stressing that the formal investigation was still under way. âOur understanding is heâs going to be transferred to the UAE,â the Israeli official said. âWe will be part of that investigation.â Netanyahu said the co-pilot appeared to have exploited a loophole in Israeli aviation rules that normally bar pilots from flying to Israel if they are from countries that do not have diplomatic relations with Israel. Oman does not have diplomatic relations with Israel. Netanyahu had also warned in recent days of heightened security threats but told CNN that Israel had received no specific warning related to the flight incident. US raises possible Iran link US President Donald Trump has raised the possibility of an Iranian connection to the attack, although he has not provided evidence and said the investigation was still under way. Asked at the White House whether he had been briefed about links between the co-pilot and Tehran, Trump said, âWeâre working on it right now.â âI would say the answer, based on what Iâm hearing, is yes, but weâre working on it right now,â he said. Trump did not elaborate on why he suspected Iran might be involved. Asked whether the US would retaliate against Tehran if Iran was behind the attack, Trump said, âOh theyâll be hit, very hard, donât worry.â âYou just ask them,â he added. âThey know what happened. Theyâll be hit very hard.â Netanyahu, however, said it was too early to establish Iranian involvement. Trump's comments came as diplomatic efforts to end the seven-month US-Iran war appeared to have stalled. Passengers got into cockpit to take control of jet Passengers on the plane have described how the bloodied Indian captain, Smit Machchhar, managed to open the cockpit door after being attacked, allowing passengers to enter and grapple with the co-pilot. The passengers then helped stabilise the aircraft after it went into an extremely steep descent. The manoeuvre was so severe that the aircraft's rudder was reportedly torn away. âWe felt helpless, suspended in midair, and I didnât know who to turn to. But it was all instinct to survive,â Asaf Rajuan, one of the passengers who intervened, said in a statement shared by the Israeli presidency. The regional official said the suspect, an Omani citizen, was under arrest before being handed over to the UAE. Saudi authorities were working with Israel and other countries to determine his motive. Captain Machchhar, who was widely praised as one of the heroes of the flight, was recovering in Abu Dhabi, the Indian government said Thursday. The weapon used by the co-pilot has not been publicly identified. Distress codes sent from cockpit Someone in the cockpit sent two four-digit codes while the plane was flying erratically near the Jordanian border with Saudi Arabia, according to Flightradar24.com. The first code was â7700â, the universal squawk code for an emergency. It was followed by â7500â, which indicates unlawful interference, including a possible hijacking. Such codes can be used by pilots when it is impossible or dangerous to communicate verbally over the radio. Flydubai said the jet was secured by on-duty crew members âwho diverted and landed the aircraft safelyâ. A regional official said those crew members were pilots in training. In the chaos that began about two and a half hours after takeoff, the Boeing 737 Max 8 descended from 33,000 feet to 17,000 feet, or around 10,000 metres to 5,100 metres, in about a minute, before making an erratic circle close to the Jordanian border and landing in Tabuk. The flight was carrying 182 people, most of them Israelis, along with passengers from India and the UAE. The US State Department said four passengers were American citizens. You use AI every day. title: Palestinian-born US mosque leader faces deportation after judge rules he is âforeign policy threatâ
text: Sarsour, president of the Islamic Society of Milwaukee, was detained by ICE officers in March. A US immigration judge has ruled that Salah Sarsour, the Palestinian-born leader of Wisconsinâs largest mosque, can be deported on grounds that he poses a foreign policy threat, while rejecting allegations that he lied on his green card application. According to The Associated Press, Sarsour, president of the Islamic Society of Milwaukee, was detained by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers in Milwaukee in March. A federal judge ordered his release in June, saying he had raised a âsubstantialâ claim that the Trump administration may have targeted him for speaking out against Israel and advocating for Palestinian rights. Sarsour said the latest ruling was âdeeply disappointingâ and that he plans to appeal. âI will continue fighting to defend the right to free speech and to stay in the country I have called home for more than three decades,â he said. The US government has argued that Sarsourâs decades-old terrorism-related convictions in Israel make him a national security threat and alleged that he concealed them while applying for a green card. Immigration Judge Jayme Salinardi agreed that Sarsour could be deported on foreign-policy grounds but rejected the allegation that he lied on his application, AP reported. Sarsour fears deportation to West Bank could cost him his life Sarsour was born in the Israeli-occupied West Bank and has lived in the US since 1993. He was imprisoned in Israel in 1988 after confessing to throwing a Molotov cocktail and stones at Israeli military personnel. In 1995, he was convicted of attempting to possess weapons and ammunition. Sarsour denies committing the offences. His lawyers have argued that he was tortured and coerced into confessing by Israeli authorities. Sarsour does not have a criminal record in the US. His lawyers also say US authorities have known about his convictions in Israel for decades and that he never concealed the information from immigration officials. âIf I am sent back to the West Bank, it means the end of my life,â Sarsour told AP in an interview on Tuesday. His attorney Patrick Taurel said Sarsourâs previous treatment by Israeli authorities could indicate what he might face if deported. Lawyer says Sarsour will appeal deportation ruling Taurel said Sarsour was being unfairly targeted and would challenge the deportation order. âIf Salah can be deported for his speech in support of Palestinian rights, anyone can face the same fate,â Taurel said, according to AP. The case comes after Secretary of State Marco Rubio issued a memo in June 2025 saying Sarsour could be deported on similar grounds used against Palestinian rights advocates Mahmoud Khalil and Mohsen Mahdawi, according to court documents cited by AP. Sarsour's legal team is expected to argue that he could face torture if returned to the West Bank. Taurel acknowledged that proving such a claim would be difficult but said Sarsourâs previous experience and Israelâs treatment of similarly situated Palestinians could support the case. Sarsour's lawyers have also questioned why US authorities detained him only this year despite allegedly knowing about his past in Israel for decades. Jawad Boulos, who represented Sarsour during his Israeli case, testified that he was coerced into confessing and was not convicted of an offence linking him to a terrorist organisation. Other witnesses, including Sarsourâs brother, also testified about his physical condition and alleged mistreatment while in Israeli custody. The Israeli government rejects allegations of abuse and wrongdoing in its treatment of Palestinian prisoners. A US federal judge had ordered Sarsour's release from ICE custody in June while his immigration case continued. The judge said Sarsour could have a valid claim that the government had retaliated against him for exercising his free speech rights and noted that ICE and the Department of Homeland Security had not adequately explained why he was suddenly considered a threat after decades of legal residency. The Trump administration has appealed that decision. Sarsour also lost more than 30 pounds while in ICE custody, according to his lawyers, who raised concerns about his medical treatment. An AP and KFF Health News investigation found that hundreds of immigration detainees across at least 33 states had filed federal lawsuits alleging medical neglect. Sarsour is among several people arrested in the US and threatened with deportation after publicly supporting Palestinians since the Israel-Hamas war began in October 2023. You use AI every day. title: Flydubai co-pilot likely acted alone; Israeli probe finds no terror link for now - report
text: Hamam al-Hammami, the accused co-pilot in the flydubai incident (Image source: LinkedIn) New reports suggest that the Omani co-pilot accused of attacking the captain and trying to seize control of a Flydubai flight bound for Tel Aviv probably acted alone. An Israeli official told CNN that information gathered during the investigation so far suggested Hamam al-Hammami acted alone. Another Israeli source said Israel had found no known link between the suspect and any group or government, while stressing that the investigation was still ongoing. The development comes as investigators examine whether al-Hammami made a further attempt to bring down the Boeing 737 after his initial attack on Captain Smit Machchhar failed. An investigation by Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera , cited by Ynet News, said investigators were examining whether the co-pilot moved the aircraft's two engine fuel switches from âRunâ to âCutoffâ after taking control of the plane. According to the report, al-Hammami allegedly pushed the aircraft into a steep descent after disabling the autopilot, potentially attempting to crash it in the Saudi desert after passengers and crew began thwarting his attempt to seize the aircraft. What happened inside the cockpit The incident took place on September 30 aboard Flydubai flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv. Al-Hammami allegedly attacked Machchhar with a cockpit crash axe and attempted to take control of the aircraft. Despite being wounded, Machchhar managed to activate the mechanism that opened the cockpit door, allowing cabin crew and passengers to enter and help subdue the co-pilot. The aircraft eventually made an emergency landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia. The UAE attorney general has described the incident as an attempted âterrorist actâ. Investigations are being conducted by authorities in the UAE, Israel and Saudi Arabia. US president Donald Trump had earlier suggested that al-Hammami could be linked to Iran, saying it was âbased on what Iâm hearingâ. He did not provide details. Israeli sources now say they have not identified a link to any group or government, although the investigation has not concluded. Questions over his past Al-Hammami, 29, is an Omani national who had previously worked for Oman Air. According to CNN, he was removed from his previous job after concerns about his extremist views. He later joined Flydubai and had been working there for around eight months. Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu has separately said al-Hammami had undergone âIslamist radical indoctrinationâ, based on information gathered during questioning. He did not provide further details. The investigation has also raised questions over aviation security and the vetting of foreign flight crews. CNN reported that the names of all passengers and crew had been provided to Israeli authorities before the flight took off. Israel's tax authority confirmed receiving the list, but the transportation ministry said its protocols did not include checking the names of flight crew members. The issue is particularly sensitive because Oman does not have formal diplomatic relations with Israel. Netanyahu has said Israel had longstanding arrangements aimed at preventing pilots from countries without diplomatic ties from flying into the country and described the case as exposing a âloopholeâ. title: âQuagmireâ over: Trump hails US exit from Iraq after 12-year ISIS mission
text: Trump described the withdrawal, completed by the September 30 deadline, as the end of what he called 'a very expensive excursion into Hell' US President Donald Trump on Wednesday hailed the withdrawal of American troops from Iraq as an âorderlyâ end to a 12-year mission against the Islamic State group, as the last US forces left an air base in northern Iraq under a deal between Washington and Baghdad. Trump described the withdrawal, completed by the September 30 deadline, as the end of what he called âa very expensive excursion into Hellâ. At a White House event, he said the US involvement in Iraq had resulted from âvery bad decision makingâ and called the conflict a âquagmireâ that had lasted for many years. âIt's been a long time with very bad decision making that got us involved in this quagmire in the first place. It was a quagmire. For many, many years it lasted. But soon that part of history will be over,â Trump said. Watch âBig ISIS Plot Amid Iran War!â: Trump Spills Iraq âSecretâ After U.S. Troops Exit Middle East He said the withdrawal represented a victory for the US and Iraq and marked a victory over the Islamic State group. US shifts to Iraqi-led security Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said US troops and equipment had completed an âorderly departureâ from the air base in Irbil in Iraq's semi-autonomous Kurdish region. âThis milestone reflects the success of a 12-year campaign that defeated ISIS as an organised military threat in Iraq and across the region,â Parnell said. âIt also marks a transition from a wartime coalition mission to an Iraqi-led security effort supported by a more normal bilateral security relationship.â He said the US military would continue to provide âtargeted training and intelligence supportâ to Iraqi partners. Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi presided over the handover ceremony and described the withdrawal as the start of a ânew phaseâ centred on Iraq's sovereignty and stronger institutions. He said Iraqi security forces would continue fighting Islamic State and that the government would ensure non-state groups no longer held weapons. Withdrawal comes amid Iran war The US exit comes as Washington remains engaged in a war with Iran that has also spilled into Iraq. Iran-backed Iraqi militias have attacked US positions, while the US has carried out strikes against militia strongholds. Bases in the Kurdish region have faced repeated attacks since the US and Israel launched their war against Iran on February 28. Trump also compared the Iraq conflict with his administration's military actions in Iran, arguing that the Iran war and a one-day US operation in Venezuela earlier this year had taken less time and resulted in fewer US military deaths. The withdrawal also reflects Washington's broader effort in recent years to shift its strategic focus from the Middle East towards Asia. That shift has been complicated by renewed US military involvement in the region. US presence in Iraq dates back to 2003 The US invaded Iraq in 2003 to overthrow Saddam Hussein and withdrew its forces in 2011. Three years later, Baghdad invited a smaller US-led mission to help fight Islamic State after the group seized large areas of Iraq. As the group was reduced to scattered sleeper cells, Washington and Baghdad agreed in 2024 to wind down the mission. Most US troops left Iraqi bases last year, leaving several hundred in the semi-autonomous Kurdish region until Wednesday's final withdrawal. The departure was welcomed by Iran-backed groups but has also raised concerns in parts of Iraq, particularly the Kurdish region, over the possibility of renewed Islamic State attacks and further strikes by Iran-linked groups. Questions remain over Iraqi militias The future of Iraq's powerful armed groups remains uncertain. Baghdad had initially linked the September 30 US withdrawal deadline to the disarmament of non-state militias. Some smaller groups agreed to hand over their weapons, but powerful Iran-aligned militias rejected the move or imposed conditions. Al-Zaidi has since pushed the disarmament deadline to June 2027, according to an interview with The New York Times earlier this month. The Kurdish regional government's Peshmerga Ministry said the region had faced more than 1,000 drone and ballistic-missile attacks during the recent US-Iran conflict. It expressed concern over the departure of US forces and the removal of American air defence systems. Iran-backed groups, meanwhile, celebrated the US withdrawal. Kataib Hezbollah security official Abu Mujahid al-Assaf called the departure âthe beginning of full sovereigntyâ but warned the Iraqi government against carrying out what he described as American plans. The Islamic Resistance in Iraq, an umbrella group of Iran-backed militias, said it was ânot bound by any timeline or agreementâ announced by the government or political groups, while saying it remained open to dialogue over weapons and Iraq's sovereignty.
