title: Beyond diplomacy: Blood, bravery, and the bond between nations
text: For decades, official relations between India and Israel were characterized by distance and diplomatic estrangement. However, under the leadership of Prime Minister Narendra Modi, India has undergone a profound awakening, shedding outdated ideological burdens that no longer served its national interest to make room for truth, strategic alignment, and genuine partnership. Yet, while diplomatic and defense ties have flourished at the state level, the history of international relations shows that the deepest bonds between peoples are ultimately forged not in conference rooms, but in raw, unscripted moments of human solidarity. Bonds between nations are truly sealed when citizens face the brink of death together. Moments of mortal peril possess a unique power to catalyze connections between societies for three fundamental reasons. First, they distill pure humanity: when facing immediate mortality, all national, religious, and political divides vanish. Second, they create an eternal moral debt: a nation whose citizen rescues another from death establishes a bond of honor that lasts for generations. Finally, they offer a narrative of hope, a living proof that even in the darkest hours, human solidarity can triumph over hatred. This fundamental truth was etched into history aboard a Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv, when an attempted hijacked air disaster, what could have been the most tragic aviation catastrophe in Israel's history, was averted through extraordinary bravery. At 34,000 feet, the plane, carrying nearly 180 passengers, became the target of a violent terrorist attack. Captain Smit Machchhar, an Indian pilot and former SpiceJet aviator with over 13 years of commercial flying experience, found himself fighting for control of the aircraft after being stabbed. Bleeding and under attack, Captain Machchhar he recited Hanuman Chalisa the equvant to Jewish Shema Yisrael to ask a divine protection in unreal situation. In a conversation with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu following the incident, Captain Machchhar shared that in those harrowing moments, he simply realized that if he did not unlock the cockpit door, it would be the end for everyone on board. He held on to a single hope: that if he could muster one final effort to unlock the door, someone outside would step in. As he noted, he knew he had âone last pushâ left in him. That final push was met with immediate action. Israeli passengers, alongside two deadheading pilots, saw death at their doorstep and broke into the cockpit, neutralized the terrorist and secured the aircraft. Much like the civilian heroes of October 7th who rose up to rebuild a nation in the wake of systemic failure, ordinary people on that flight saved nearly 180 lives. This was not merely an Israeli story. It was a stark reminder that the war against terror is ultimately fought by ordinary citizens who bear the costs. Symbolically, the seamless cooperation between an Indian captain fighting with his last breath and Israeli passengers storming the cockpit serves as a metaphor for global hope: two ancient civilizations standing together to defend human dignity against jihadist terror. Given the complex national security challenges our countries continuously face, we at least know how to honor our heroes. For his valor, Captain Machchhar deserves Indiaâs highest peacetime military decoration, the Ashoka Chakra. In recognition of this heroic act, Prime Minister Netanyahu invited Captain Machchhar to visit Israel and light a torch at the next national Independence Day ceremony, an honor reserved for those who embody exceptional bravery, civic devotion, or extraordinary service to the country and humanity. The relationship between Israelis and Indians has evolved dramatically in recent years. For decades, the average Israeliâs perception of India was shaped primarily by a handful of postmilitary backpackers returning from remote villages with stories of spiritual journeys. However, the period following October 7th revealed the true depth of this connection. As parts of Europe allowed centuries of latent antisemitism to resurface under new guises, millions of Indian citizens voluntarily took to digital spaces to defend Israel against coordinated influence operations from Iran, Qatar, and Turkey. No other nation understands the reality of living under the threat of Islamist terror better than India. Both countries recognize that terrorism often disguises itself with false justifications while inciting deadly violence against innocent civilians. Recently, when India experienced a brutal terrorist attack in Kashmir, an attack inspired by the tactics used on October 7th, which escalated regional tensions and led to India's defensive response in Operation Sindoor , Israel stood firmly by India without any hesitation. The extraordinary rescue aboard the Flydubai flight was more than an act of professional duty, it reflected the indomitable spirit of two peoples bound by an unyielding faith in justice, truth, and the resolve to confront darkness together. India and Israel must realize that this joint struggle against terror may well be the âone last pushâ required before clarity and security are restored to the international order. Dr. Oshrit Birvadker is a senior national security analyst and the director of the South and East Asia Center at the Jerusalem Center for Strategy and Security (JISS). title: The vetting gap: How an Omani flagged for extremism ended up piloting a Tel Aviv-bound flydubai jet
text: Hamam al-Hammami, the accused co-pilot in the flydubai incident (Image source: LinkedIn) Hamam al-Hammami, the Omani co-pilot accused of stabbing Captain Smit Machchhar and attempting to crash a flydubai flight bound for Tel Aviv, had already come to the attention of authorities for his radical extremist tendencies. Despite this he was cleared to fly to Israel by flydubai. Investigators are trying to establish how an Omani pilot ended up as first officer on a flight to Israel, given that Israel and Oman do not have diplomatic relations. Hamam al-Hammami's background Al-Hammami is a 29-year-old Omani national, according to US media reports. He entered pilot training with Oman Air and worked for the airline for several years. A LinkedIn profile bearing his name, which CNN said was verified by a source as belonging to him, showed a seven-year stint at Oman Air ending in February 2025. It also listed a subsequent job with Royal Air Maroc, from June 2025 to January 2026. The profile has since been deleted. Investigators are also examining social-media material attributed to al-Hammami. A deleted video showed Israeli aircraft in Dubai and ended with images of former al-Qaeda leader Ayman al-Zawahiri and al-Qaeda-linked suicide bomber Humam Khalil Abu-Mulal al-Balawi. Another post featured an AI-generated image of Mecca, Medina and Jerusalem accompanied by a poem about rejecting humiliation and not fearing death. CNN said it remained unclear who posted the material or whether the posts had been scheduled as they were posted after the flydubai incident. CNN also analysed thousands of deleted posts attributed to al-Hammami, including material expressing strongly misogynistic and conservative views. How did he get into the cockpit? The question about his presence on a flight headed towards Tel Aviv arose because Oman does not have diplomatic relations with Israel, yet al-Hammami was serving as a co-pilot on a Dubai-Tel Aviv flight operated by a UAE airline. Israeli authorities are investigating how he came to be assigned to the flight and whether aviation-security procedures were followed. CBS News reported that sources initially suggested al-Hammami could have held dual citizenship, which they said might explain how he was cleared to fly to Israel. He was born in the UAE to an Omani father and Syrian mother and spent much of his life outside Oman, according to sources cited by CNN. However, a later report by Jerusalem Post citing people familiar with the investigation said he did not have a second nationality, leaving the question of how he was cleared unresolved. According to sources cited by CBS News, Omani government surveillance found that al-Hammami was visiting radical websites while he was undergoing pilot training. Oman Air subsequently transferred him from flying duties to an administrative role. One source said he later resigned from the airline after being placed on desk duty and left around 2024. Other reports have described him as having been barred or suspended from flying in Oman over concerns about his extremist views. After leaving Oman Air, al-Hammami moved to Dubai and eventually joined flydubai. Sources told CBS News that flydubai hired him without vetting him through the Omani government. That has become one of the central questions in the investigation: whether information about his earlier removal from flying duties was passed on to his subsequent employers or relevant security authorities. It remains unclear what background checks were conducted when he joined flydubai. What are investigators probing now? Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said investigators believe al-Hammami underwent Islamist radicalisation and was trying to crash the aircraft with its passengers. He has also said authorities are examining whether he was sent by someone else. US president Donald Trump separately suggested that al-Hammami could be linked to Iran, although Netanyahu has said it was too early to determine whether Iran was involved. The UAE has opened an investigation into whether the attack involved terrorist activity, prior planning or outside direction, while Israeli authorities are examining how al-Hammami came to be part of the flight crew. title: Peacemaker with a warning to annihilate: The major contradictions in Trump's UN speech
text: Donald Trump used much of his address at the UN to list his achievements. (AP photo) US President Donald Trump returned to the United Nations podium Tuesday wearing two very different hats. One moment he was the global peacemaker who had "ended eight wars", the next he was threatening to wipe out Iran. The gap between these two versions captures the uncertain order Trump has built, or perhaps enabled, during his second term in the White House. Trump used much of his address to the General Debate of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly to list his achievements, much as he did a year ago when he cast himself as the standout contender for the Nobel Peace Prize. This year, though, the prize went unmentioned. Instead, his tone hardened, with attacks on the International Criminal Court (ICC), the UN's climate agenda and Unesco. Trump also pointed to his effort to launch a "Board of Peace" in January, which appeared another swipe at the UN, with him at one point suggesting his new creation might end up replacing it. Watch ðºð¸ United States of America - President Addresses United Nations General Debate, 81st Session Ironically, within a month of the board's creation, the US and Israel launched a joint military operation against Iran, one that has continued in some form since. "Since I took office, it has been my great honour to settle eight wars, and in so doing, become friendly with the leaders of many of those countries. It was a great honour to do it. Numerous of these wars have gone on for many years and even decades," he told the assembled leaders. He credited his success to what he called "very special relationships", along with the use and threat of tariffs. Among the conflicts he claimed to have resolved were the disputes between Cambodia and Thailand, Kosovo and Serbia, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Rwanda, Pakistan and India, and Armenia and Azerbaijan, as well as the war in Gaza. He repeated a claim India has long rejected, that he brokered peace between India and Pakistan last year. "The Prime Minister of Pakistan, terrific man, said that Donald Trump was responsible for saving 30 million lives and probably many more than that," Trump said. India has always maintained the ceasefire came from direct talks between the two countries' military operations chiefs, with Pakistani DGMO seeking the truce amid Operation Sindoor. He also mentioned Russia and Ukraine, saying his team is "working very closely" with both sides. "We will get that one done. It's going to happen, I think, more quickly than people understand," he said. Peacemaker to annihilator Having spent much of the speech basking in the image of a dealmaker, Trump turned to Iran, warning that Tehran must either negotiate with Washington or face destruction. Iran would never be allowed to have nuclear weapons, he said, adding that he faces "a big decision to make." "Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before, maybe one of the greatest in the Middle East or even the world? Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic, and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?" He went further still, asking, "Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?" He then predicted a deal was more likely once the midterm elections were over, since Iran was "waiting to see how I do in the midterm election," despite Trump not being on the ballot himself. Lo and behold, Trump's speech offered a portrait of a President who saw no contradiction in claiming the mantle of peacemaker while reserving the language of annihilation for those who resist his terms. title: Camp David huddle: Trump team discusses Iran war, possible Yemen offensive - report
text: File photo: Houthi supporters shout slogans during a rally against Israel and the United States' war on Iran, in Sanaa, Yemen US president Donald Trumpâs top national security aides met secretly at Camp David on Friday for several hours to discuss the war with Iran and the Saudi-backed push against Houthi rebels in Yemen, three US officials told Axios. The meeting was not announced by the Trump administration and came as negotiations with Iran remained stalled, with Trump weighing whether to resume major combat operations against Tehran. Vice president JD Vance chaired the meeting, according to the officials. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, White House envoy Steve Witkoff, CIA director John Ratcliffe and chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen Dan Caine were among those who attended. âThings were decided or at least deeply discussed,â one US official said, referring to the Middle East crisis. The White House did not comment on the meeting. Iran talks and a possible return to combat The meeting came as Trump faces a decision over the future of the US campaign against Iran. With negotiations stalled, Trump has been considering whether to resume major combat operations. On Thursday, he issued a stark warning over the talks, saying: âNow I have to make a decision: either Iran signs the deal, or it wonât exist any longer.â Trump was asked about his next move on Iran on Friday afternoon while his advisers were meeting at Camp David. âIf I told you, you would have a major story,â Trump told reporters. âBut you will see. It is working out very well. Iran is not doing well.â The Camp David discussions also covered the escalating Saudi-Houthi conflict in Yemen. Saudi Arabia is preparing a possible offensive against the Houthis and has been urging Trump to support the campaign with US airstrikes. Trump has so far been leaning against joining the operation, although US officials said he could change his position. title: AI sings Russia's war story: Inside the rise of generative songs about Ukraine conflict
text: Among the songs whose release dates could be established, most appeared after 2024. (Reuters photo) Artificial intelligence is being used to produce a growing number of songs about the Russia-Ukraine war, with some of the music presenting Russia's invasion in a favourable light and criticising Ukraine. Hundreds of such tracks have appeared on major music streaming platforms, including Spotify, Apple Music, YouTube and Deezer, according to research by Terrecon, a Ukrainian nonprofit organisation focused on threat intelligence. The songs cover a wide range of musical styles, from ballads to heavy metal. Terrecon said some praise Russian soldiers, describe the war from a Russian perspective and contain derogatory references to Ukrainians, including ethnic slurs. One of the more popular tracks identified by the organisation is âPower of Artilleryâ, a Russian-language rock song centred on artillery systems including Krasnopol and Carnation. Nearly 1,000 songs identified Terrecon said it catalogued 981 songs created with AI that contained what it classified as pro-Russian war propaganda. Among the songs whose release dates could be established, most appeared after 2024. That coincided with the wider availability of AI music generators such as Sudo and Udio. The technology has lowered the time and cost involved in producing music, according to Daria Verbytska, a founder of Terrecon. âThey have found new ways to create cheaper drones and use them on a massive scale,â Daria Verbytska, a founder of Terrecon, said told NYT in a telephone interview, referring to the Russians. âItâs like that with music â creating massive propaganda with the help of AIâ Some of the songs use themes associated with Soviet-era war music but present them through contemporary genres. One track, âSoldier's Daughterâ, describes the death of a soldier and the impact on his child while also portraying the soldier's sacrifice in a positive light. It is not clear how much involvement, if any, the Russian government has had in producing or distributing the songs. However, the Kremlin has supported cultural projects aimed at promoting patriotic themes. Last week, a director of Moscow's Internet Development Institute, an organisation that works closely with the Kremlin to promote patriotic values, said in a presentation that the institute had supported more than 350 artistic projects related to the war, according to Russian media reports. AI tools can produce war-related music Terrecon also tested several AI music generators to see how they responded to prompts requesting songs promoting Russian views of the war. Researchers used Suno, Udio and Google Flow Music in the US, along with Singapore-based Mureka. They entered prompts in both Russian and English, including requests involving violence and derogatory descriptions. The platforms rejected some prompts, but researchers said they were nevertheless able to generate songs resembling some of those in Terrecon's database. They then uploaded the tracks to YouTube Music and SoundCloud. âThe moderation systems mainly responded to specific banned words rather than the overall meaning of the prompts,â Terreconâs report found. The researchers said the issue is partly linked to the differing rules adopted by AI music services and streaming platforms. They also said automated systems may have difficulty identifying expressions, slang and offensive language in different languages. Streaming platforms tighten AI rules Major music platforms generally have policies covering hate speech and violent content, although fewer have specific rules dealing with propaganda. Deezer and YouTube are among the platforms that require certain AI-generated content to be labelled. Spotify said in September that it had introduced a policy to label AI-generated songs and prevent them from being recommended to users. The company also added labels to songs shared by The New York Times as examples. Terrecon said the songs it identified had been played millions of times across major streaming services, although the extent to which listeners understood that some of the music was AI-generated or politically motivated is unclear. Deezer spokesman Jesper Wendel said the platform reviews potentially rule-breaking content on a case-by-case basis. SoundCloud spokeswoman Sade Ayodele said the company reviews reported content and added that âthere is no place on SoundCloud for content that incites or glorifies violence.â The emergence of these songs illustrates how AI music tools can be used to produce and distribute large volumes of war-related material. It also presents streaming and AI companies with the challenge of deciding how existing rules on hate speech, violence, political content and AI-generated material should apply to such music. title: Saudi Arabia has not ruled out developing nuclear weapons, classified US assessment warns
text: Saudi nuclear weapons option not off the table The US Congress has reportedly received a classified intelligence assessment warning that Saudi Arabia has not ruled out developing a nuclear weapons programme, according to a report by The Washington Post. The assessment comes after Washington and Riyadh confirmed in July that they had reached an agreement that could potentially allow Saudi Arabia to develop uranium enrichment capabilities as part of its civilian nuclear programme. The agreement has raised concerns among US lawmakers from both parties and Israeli officials over the possibility that Saudi Arabia could eventually use the technology to develop nuclear weapons. However, the Republican-controlled US legislature does not appear likely to block its implementation. A group of Democratic senators, led by Massachusetts Senator Ed Markey and Oregon Senator Jeff Merkley, wrote to Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Friday, warning that the departure from established precedent could set in motion a process âthat is all but certain to allow Riyadh to acquire the means to enrich uranium and possibly develop nuclear weapons.â Watch MBS's Troops 'BOMBED' In Surprise Attack By Houthis; Saudi Ally Soldiers Hit In Yemen's Jazan Merkley called the situation âbogus as hellâ, arguing that Saudi Arabiaâs demands indicated that its nuclear programme could extend beyond civilian purposes. âIf theyâve given up the intent to develop a nuclear weapon, then theyâd give up domestic enrichment and reprocessing power, right? Theyâd accept massive inspections from the IAEA,â he said. Markey linked his concerns to the ongoing war with Iran, noting that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman had previously warned that Riyadh would seek to develop a nuclear bomb if Tehran did so. âIt is very clear that as this war in Iran continues to unfold, that the Iranians are going to fiercely defend their ability to develop a nuclear weapons program, and as a result, any action that we take in Saudi Arabia will only further accelerate a fallout nuclear arms race in the region,â Markey said. The Democratic senatorsâ letter also criticised Trump administration officials whom they said stood to benefit from the agreement. âJared Kushner, for example, accepted a $2 billion investment from a Saudi sovereign wealth fund after leaving the White House at the end of the first Trump Administration,â the report said. âWestinghouse Electric, meanwhile, stands to make tens of billions of dollars if this agreement moves forward. Westinghouseâs majority owner is closely associated with Newmark, the real estate firm run and owned in part by the sons of Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.â Under the agreement, US businesses will participate in developing nuclear power projects in Saudi Arabia, a move expected to boost the US nuclear power industry and strengthen ties between the two countries. The 30-year agreement gives US companies a central role in developing Saudi Arabiaâs civilian nuclear infrastructure, largely excluding foreign competitors. Saudi Arabia will be allowed to enrich uranium to nearly 20 per cent under the agreement, well below the level required to make a nuclear weapon, as cited by The New York Times. However, uranium enriched to that level could be further enriched to weapons-grade material within a relatively short period. The agreement comes against the backdrop of wider concerns over a potential nuclear arms race in the Middle East. Israel is an undeclared nuclear power, while Iran has long pursued uranium enrichment, one of the reasons the United States attacked Iran in February. You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. title: Trump's 48 F-35 jets for Saudi Arabia: Why is Israel uneasy and China a key concern
text: US President Donald Trump with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman during a âcoffee ceremonyâ at the Saudi Royal Court on May 13, 2025, in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. The Trump administration has agreed to put the world's most advanced combat aircraft in Saudi hands. It comes at a time when Gulf allies are questioning whether American primacy still carries weight. And nowhere is that question more important than in the ever-conflicted region of West Asia. Washington's approach to West Asia has long resembled digging a hole to bury sand, only to be left with a new heap of sand, creating a loop that keeps the digging going. Trump's decision to approve the $24.3 billion sale of F-35s to the Saudis, when the Kingdom is being bogged down by the Iran-backed Houthis, appears to be the latest turn of the spade. Though it is meant to steady a Gulf partner shaken by Iranian fire and doubts about American guarantees, the aircraft deal has opened a fresh cavity for Israel, until now the only country in the region to fly the world's most powerful combat aircraft. Under the deal, the state department has notified Congress of a possible sale of 48 jets, with engines and support, which would make Saudi Arabia the second country in the Middle East to fly the aircraft after Israel. However, the Saudi jets will reportedly not have all the advanced features of the F-35s operated by Israel. The F-35I, also known as the Adir, a custom variant based on the Alpha, redesigned, and modified by the Israeli Defence Force (IDF). Although strictly forbidden, after negotiations the US defence force reluctantly gave permission for Israeli designers to make certain modifications to the F-35A design. The F-35I â also known as the Adir â a custom variant based on the Alpha, redesigned, and modified by the Israeli Defence Force. Production and delivery would take years, but the political signal is immediate, with some Israeli officials raising concerns that the deal could erode their country's "qualitative military edge" -- a standard that American policymakers have sought to protect since the 1973 war and that Congress has mandated. Numbers not the real worry Israel bought 50 F-35s in two rounds, in 2016 and 2017, although several reports suggest two have yet to arrive. That leaves 48 on the ground, the same number Riyadh has requested. However, Israel will not stay level for long, since its defence ministry plans 25 more jets from 2028 and has announced a further squadron of unspecified size. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, however, reportedly played down its significance of Trump's deal with Saudi Arabia. The anxiety is therefore about something less measurable. When Donald Trump first confirmed he was considering the sale last November, Israeli officials told Axios they did not oppose it as such, but wanted it "to be subject to Saudi normalisation with Israel". That condition has not been met, and no such deal appears close. A security source told CNN at the time that Saudi Arabia acquiring "the same capabilities" was "very concerning". Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, however, reportedly played down its significance. Presence of US bases across Middle East. Meanwhile, Washington has maintained that regional balance will hold as "the proposed sale of this equipment and support will not alter the military balance in the region". Interestingly, whether Israel accepts that assurance will depend less on the wording than on who Riyadh chooses to stand with in the years ahead. China's shadow over the deal The strongest objection in Washington concerns Beijing, with a defense intelligence agency assessment, issued months ago, questioning whether American and Saudi personnel could secure the sites that would hold F-35 technology. It also flagged the access Chinese military personnel have to Saudi bases and the kingdom's heavy use of Chinese telecommunications technology in its infrastructure and defence installations. An earlier assessment had already questioned the growing partnership, in which China sells Saudi Arabia ballistic missiles and helps it learn to build them. Representative Raja Krishnamoorthi, a Democrat on the House Intelligence Committee, put the fear plainly. "It could put the crown jewels of American military technology within reach of the Chinese Communist Party," he said. US President Donald Trump and Saudi Crown Prince and Prime Minister Mohammed bin Salman laugh during a meeting in the Oval Office at the White House in Washington, November 18, 2025. There is also a precedent when Trump announced an F-35 sale to the United Arab Emirates (UAE) in 2020, and the Biden administration ended the process over similar worries about Abu Dhabi's links with China. For Israel, the risk is indirect; it's highly unlikely that Riyadh, which is absorbing Iranian missile and drone attacks, would hand secrets to Tehran. The concern is leakage through third parties. The US intelligence agencies worry that Chinese spies could target Saudi networks, maintenance sites and personnel, a task made easier by Chinese military personnel's access to Saudi bases and by Chinese technology in the Kingdom's telecommunications and defence installations. The burden of broken promises Understanding why Riyadh might gradually hedge against America in the future, potentially against Israel's interests, helps trace how American security promises have fared over the years. The 2003 invasion of Iraq, launched with great confidence in what military force could achieve, ended in a costly occupation and shook the regional order, though that order eventually reassembled. In 2011, the fall of Egypt's Hosni Mubarak convinced Arab autocrats they could not count on Washington to save them from domestic upheaval. Several set out to contain threats themselves, often with devastating results. Doubts about deterrence against Iran grew denser after Washington did not respond to a 2019 attack on Saudi oil refineries attributed to Iran, and Houthi drone strikes on the UAE in 2022 deepened the unease. The 2026 war with Iran did the most damage as Gulf leaders were seemingly angry that the United States and Israel launched it without consulting them, in the middle of Omani-brokered talks with Tehran. Iran struck every Gulf state but concentrated on Bahrain and the UAE, both Abraham Accords signatories. Missile defences stopped the worst, yet enough got through to cause real harm, and much of the network of American bases was damaged, destroyed or rendered irrelevant. Washington then failed to dislodge the Iranian regime and could not keep the Strait of Hormuz open. American strikes on Iranian water storage facilities, and Israeli strikes on oil depots, alarmed Gulf capitals that feared reprisals against their own water and nuclear sites. Even Riyadh's long-sought nuclear agreement was left in limbo when Trump changed its terms a day after it was finalised. Moreover, Mohammed bin Salman, the Kingdom's Crown Prince, is reportedly unhappy with Trump's refusal to provide direct military support to Saudi Arabia in its fight against the Houthis. Particarly after the its key East-West oil pipeline was hit in the attack. Yes, Saudi Arabia restarted operations at its East-West oil pipeline on September 22, 2026, after a temporary shutdown caused by drone strikes. That makes the F-35 deal look less like a favour and more like a transaction, which Trump has ensured with all his key allies, even Europe. Summing up that sentiment, retired US Lieutenant General Karen Gibson put it aptly: "MBS will not forget." The rival camp Riyadh has been building Before the fighting began at the end of February, Saudi Arabia had started assembling a bloc of its own. Riyadh drew Egypt, Pakistan, Qatar and Turkey into a coalition meant to counter the American-backed Emirati-Israeli alliance. This matters a great deal for the F-35 question. The country due to receive the aircraft that anchors Israel's air power has been organising against an alignment that includes Israel. Also, Riyadh's rivalry with Abu Dhabi runs deep. Saudi Arabia backs the post-Assad government in Syria, while the UAE shares Israel's hostility towards it. In Yemen, Riyadh recently drove out Emirati proxies, and it has complained that the UAE promotes secessionist movements that undermine regional stability. Also, the UAE coordinated with Israel and the United States on strikes against Iranian targets. Riyadh watches that alignment uneasily, seeing it as a threat to its own leadership. Turkey adds another layer as Netanyahu has already called President Recep Tayyip Erdogan "not exactly a model ally of the United States", a remark he made after Trump said in July that he was weighing F-35 sales to Ankara as well. Israel thus faces advanced American jets flowing to more than one capital whose interests diverge from its own. Why Israel worries Arab allies who have lost faith in Washington, sooner or later, will increasingly exercise their autonomy, which could mean diplomacy with Iran and closer ties with China and Russia, whatever American officials prefer. Saudi Arabia has precedent here, having reached a rapprochement with Iran in 2023. Some Gulf states may now seek side deals with Tehran to stay off its target list. For a kingdom under Iranian fire, that is prudence rather than defection. Yet a fifth-generation fleet needs decades of spares, software and training, so it presumes a buyer whose alignment stays put. None of this points to an imminent break, and Gulf states may even deepen ties with Washington in the short term. A Saudi Arabia that talks to Tehran, buys Chinese missiles and uses Chinese telecommunications networks is a partner whose direction Israel cannot easily read. Congress has been given 30 days to review the sale and could pass a joint resolution of disapproval, but it would need two-thirds of both chambers to survive a veto. The House is in recess until November and the Senate is about to follow, so blocking the sale looks improbable. Any safeguards will have to be secured well before delivery. Saudi Arabia, under fire, remains by far the biggest buyer of American weapons, and interoperability with US and allied forces has genuine value. But the deeper question is whether an advanced weapon, under a purely transactional agreement, can secure loyalty against the backdrop of wobbling US guarantees? That, more than any tally of jets, is what perhaps unsettles Israel. You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

In an interview with Al-Alam News Network, Mohebbi said the IRGC had prepared for a âlong-term warâ and would respond if the conflict entered another phase of heightened hostilities. âIn our view, war is war; it has different stages, but war is war and the war is not over, the war continues, and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps has prepared itself for a long-term war, and it was ready before, and now it is even more prepared for a long-term war,â he said. title: US completes military withdrawal from Iraq after years of operations
text: The US military concludes its 12-year involvement in Iraq combating ISIS. The 12-year effort to combat, the Islamic state organization came to an end on Wednesday, when the US military declared that all of its forces had left Iraq. According to an agreement between Baghdad and Washington, American soldiers finally departed an air base in northern Iraq. The evacuation, which was decided upon two years ago, takes place in the context of the continuous conflict between the United States and Iran, which has occasionally spilled over into Iraq, with the United States attacking the militias' strongholds and Iran-backed militias shooting on American forces. Baghdad celebrated the US mission's termination as an indication of the nation's growing might and independence. Iran-backed organizations also applauded the evacuation, while some other Iraqis, especially those in the Kurdish area, expressed alarm. The future of the Iraqi militias, which the Baghdad government has attempted to disarm with limited success thus far, is a matter of concern. US personnel and equipment have completed a "orderly departure" from the air base in Irbil, in the semi-autonomous Kurdish area of northern Iraq, according to a statement from Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell. He declared, "This milestone reflects the success of a 12-year campaign that defeated ISIS as an organized military threat in Iraq and across the region." "It also signifies a change from a coalition mission during the war to an Iraqi-led security operation backed by a more regular bilateral security relationship." The US withdrawal marked the start of a "new phase, one defined by Iraq's sovereignty, the strength of its institutions, the readiness of its forces, the unity of its decision-making, and balanced partnerships with its friends," according to Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, who oversaw the handover ceremony. According to him, the government would make sure that non-state organizations no longer possess weapons, and Iraqi security forces will carry on the battle against IS. In order to overthrow Saddam Hussein, American forces invaded Iraq in 2003. The US forces withdrew in 2011, but three years later, Iraqi authorities called back a smaller US-led military mission to help combat the Islamic State group, which had seized large parts of the country during its rapid expansion. In 2024, Washington and Baghdad decided to end the campaign after the terrorist group had been reduced to dispersed sleeper cells. Last year, the majority of US outposts in Iraq were evacuated, but hundreds of troops remained in the northern Kurdish region, which is semi-autonomous. Bases there have regularly been attacked since the U.S. and Israel launched their war against Iran on Feb. 28. Iran-backed Iraqi militias have also coordinated attacks against Saudi Arabia with Yemen's Houthi rebels. Iraq government first linked up the Sept. 30 deadline for the withdrawal of US forces with the unconditional disarmament of non-state armed groups by that date. While a few less influential of the militias agreed to turn in their weapons, the big groups aligned with Iran either dismissed the idea or put up conditions that the government would be unlikely to agree for the meeting. Al-Zaidi later retracted the deadline. Earlier this month, he told the New York Times that the deadline for militia disarmament has been pushed to June 2027. The impact of the United States' withdrawal may not be so apparent, and it is particularly given that the United States' military power has already been reduced. Still, officials in the Iraqi Kurdish region have expressed worries over the departure and especially over the removal of the United States' air defense systems. title: Ex-officer, war widow Priyanka Saxena will be trained and reinstated as Squadron Leader: IAF chief

title: 'I watch Air Crash Investigation': How Israeli passenger controlled flydubai jet after co-pilot stabbed captain
text: Israeli passenger who controlled the plane in conversation with PM Benjamin Netanyahu An Israeli passenger, who took control of an Israel-bound flydubai passenger jet after its pilot was stabbed and wounded by the co-pilot during an apparent hijacking attempt told Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that he knew how to control the aircraft because, âI watch Air Crash Investigation. â In a video posted by the Israeli Prime Ministerâs Office, the man told Netanyahu how passengers restrained the co-pilot, reportedly an Omani citizen, after the captain, an Indian national, managed to open the cockpit door despite being seriously wounded. Also Read | âIndia is proudâ: PM Modi lauds Flydubai pilot Machchhar after cockpit attack Israeli media identified the passenger as Yaniv Hayun. "I jumped back into it (the cockpit) and pulled the controls. I started pulling the...," Hayun said in Hebrew, before Netanyahu interjected: "You pulled the controls? You knew?" "Yes, because I watch Air Crash Investigations, Mr Prime Minister. And then the plane started to level out, a bit more. And then the pilot told me he was taking control from there," he added, as Netanyahu burst into laughter. Israeli media reported that two off-duty flydubai pilots who were on the flight as they were due to operate another flydubai flight then took over. The plane later made an emergency landing at Tabuk Airport in northwestern Saudi Arabia. Also Read | 'A hero': Trump hails Indian captain after Flydubai attack, calls co-pilot âperhaps a terroristâ Meanwhile, earlier in the conversation, Hayun informed Netanyahu how passengers rushed into the cockpit after the wounded captain managed to open the door. "...because of the pressure, a force like that pulled me down. And standing at the door was someone else in a white shirt, I assume it was the pilot because inside there were two pilots, and outside two pilots happened to be sitting in the cabin," Hayun said. "He and I pushed the door," the man further stated, apparently referring to another passenger. He added that the stabbed pilot was very close to the entry, making it difficult for passengers to initially break in. At this point, Netanyahu asked Hayun whether anyone had managed to open the cockpit door. The man replied in the affirmative, saying the pilot was able to open it before collapsing. Hayun then described how the plane began to descend - the jet plummeted 17,400 feet in less than two minutes, according to flight-tracking data. "The plane's nose was like this (hand gesture)â¦ I called out to the Israeli guys with us on the plane and two other guys came over to me. We pinned him (co-pilot) down to keep him (pilot) secure," he said. The Indian pilot, Captain Smit Machchhar, is undergoing treatment at a hospital in Saudi Arabia and is in stable condition, according to the Indian Embassy in Riyadh, the Saudi capital. The incident occurred just days before the third anniversary of the October 7, 2023, Hamas attacks on Israel, and amid the ongoing US-Israeli war with Iran, raising security concerns. title: Significance of the New Delhi Declaration of Brics: Intent to reshape the global order
text: Other countries too had bilateral meetings. There was also a substantive ModiâPezeshkian bilateral meeting on the sidelines of the Summit. Modi stressed that West Asian problems should be addressed through dialogue and diplomacy, and emphasised the need to ensure freedom of navigation and commerce, security of seafarers, and early return to peace. The unanimous adoption of the New Delhi Declaration at the 18th BRICS Summit was a significant diplomatic achievement for the grouping and for India as its chair. It demonstrated that BRICS is evolving from a coalition of emerging economies into a broader platform of the Global South. With its expanded membership, BRICS now represents nearly half of the world's population and around 40 per cent of global economic output, giving it substantial demographic and economic weight. This yearâs theme of âBuilding Resilience and Innovation for Cooperation and Sustainabilityâ, not only redefines the acronym BRICS but also reflected groupâs evolving aspirations and identity. The central message of the New Delhi Declaration is that the Global South is no longer prepared to remain a passive recipient of decisions taken by a few established powers. BRICS is seeking a greater role in shaping the rules and institutions of global governance in an increasingly multipolar world. The Declaration repeatedly stresses mutual respect and understanding, sovereign equality, solidarity, openness, inclusiveness, collaboration and consensus. Its stated objective is a more representative and equitable international order, a reformed multilateral system, sustainable development and inclusive growth. It is not against any alliance or nation. It focused on the need for reforms of the UN, IMF, World Bank and international financial architecture, conveying that they are not truly representing all. It emphasises that these institutions must reflect the economic and demographic realities of the 21st Century. For India, this strengthens its case for UN Security Council reform and a greater role for developing countries in global decision-making. The drafting skill helped in having a consensus. As the Foreign Ministers had failed to produce a joint statement, it appeared a daunting task. This was achieved by condemning the acts and not on the perpetrators. This was most visible on West Asia. Rather than assigning responsibility to Iran, the UAE, the US or Israel, paragraph 28 says that BRICS members, ârecalling our respective national positions,â call for âmaximum restraintâ and avoidance of actions that could aggravate the situation. It then moves to universally acceptable principlesâprotection of civilians, sovereignty, territorial integrity, dialogue and diplomacy. This separated national positions from BRICSâ emphasis on what needs to be done. It focused on broad concepts such as dialogue and diplomacy, which have growing influence globally in the current environment. Similarly, it avoided supporting any side on the Ukraine-Russia conflict. Instead, it relied on broader references to sovereignty, territorial integrity and peaceful resolution. This was a deliberate way of keeping the declaration within the common denominator acceptable to members. It demonstrated deftness in conveying the adverse impact of escalating unilateral tariff and non-tariff measures. Rather than framing trade restrictions simply as a dispute between particular countries, the declaration criticised unilateral tariff and non-tariff measures, it expressed concerns about their adverse impact on international trade and supply chains. This allowed members with different relationships with the US to agree on the broader principle. It focused on a pragmatic agenda of common interests. The declaration devotes substantial attention to issues where there is considerably greater convergence such as development and inclusive growth, reform of global governance, trade and investment, energy security, health, food security, sustainable development, supply chain resilience, AI and digital technology and climate change. The declaration sharply criticised terrorism, without naming the perpetrator. However, the message was loud and clear. It expressed strong condemnation of any acts of terrorism as criminal and unjustifiable, regardless of their motivation, whenever, wherever and by whomsoever committed. It condemned in the strongest terms the terrorist attack in Jammu and Kashmir on 22 April 2025, during which 26 people were killed and many more injured. It urged to ensure zero tolerance for terrorism and reject double standards in countering terrorism. It was stronger than last yearâs statement. Similarly, it took a strong view on the Palestinian issue. It expressed concern about the forced displacement, temporary or permanent, under any pretext, of any of the Palestinian population from the Occupied Palestinian Territory, as well as any geographic or demographic changes to the territory of the Gaza Strip. Equally important were the bilateral meetings, which included Iran, the UAE and Saudi Arabia. This demonstrated that countries involved in conflicts, could engage within BRICS. This reflects that BRICS can provide a useful diplomatic space where countries with conflicting interests continue to communicate Other countries too had bilateral meetings. There was also a substantive ModiâPezeshkian bilateral meeting on the sidelines of the Summit. Modi stressed that West Asian problems should be addressed through dialogue and diplomacy, and emphasised the need to ensure freedom of navigation and commerce, security of seafarers, and early return to peace. In addition, Modi held several bilateral meetings to strengthen relations and push for peace. Modi-Putin meeting aimed at reinforcing ties and pressing for ending the Ukraine war. His meeting with Xi Jinping was aimed at managing differences. Modi also used the BRICS platform for reinforcing its Indo-Pacific and Act East policies. His meetings with the leaders of Malaysia, Vietnam, Indonesia and the Philippines were especially geared towards these objectives. The 18th BRICS Summit indicates five salient dimensions. First, it is increasingly speaking about the Global South, rather than the original five countries. Second, its geopolitical weight has increased with expansion. Third, there is greater emphasis on the use of local currency. Fourth, despite pressures, it has remained a non-Western group and not an anti-Western entity. Fifth, it has now acquired greater bargaining power. Its greatest achievement was not the creation of a dramatic new institution, but India's ability to hold together an enlarged and internally divided grouping and give it a more practical, Global-South-oriented agenda. The broad message is that BRICS will increasingly play a role in determining the global order in the interest of the Global South and if differences can be managed, it may emerge as a counterweight to the West-led global governance system. The principal challenge, therefore, will be to preserve unity without suppressing differences, and to increase the group's influence without allowing it to become a rigid geopolitical bloc. title: What is IMEC? The India-Europe corridor in focus after Trumpâs push amid Iran tensions
text: File photo: Proposed IMEC trade route US President Donald Trump has thrown his weight behind the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC), linking the ambitious connectivity project to a broader push to move Middle Eastern energy infrastructure away from routes vulnerable to Iranian pressure. Speaking at a meeting with Gulf Cooperation Council and Arab leaders on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, Trump said attacks on commercial shipping had shown the need to shift energy infrastructure away from âIranian checkpointsâ. He said his administration âstrongly supportsâ IMEC and other efforts to create alternative routes for moving oil and energy. Trumpâs comments have brought fresh attention to a project announced with considerable fanfare at the G20 Summit in New Delhi in 2023, but whose progress has since been slowed by wars and instability across West Asia. What is IMEC? The India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor is a proposed multinational connectivity network designed to link India with the Gulf and Europe through a combination of sea, rail, road, energy and digital infrastructure. The project has two broad sections: an Eastern Corridor, connecting India to the Arabian Gulf, and a Northern Corridor, connecting the Gulf to Europe. The proposed network would combine maritime shipping with rail and road links rather than relying entirely on a single mode of transport. The plan also envisages electricity infrastructure, digital connectivity and potentially hydrogen-related infrastructure alongside the transport network. The corridor was announced at the September 2023 G20 Summit in New Delhi. Its core participants include India, the US, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Israel, Jordan, France, Germany, Italy and the European Union. At its core, IMEC is intended to make the movement of goods, energy and data between India, the Middle East and Europe faster and more resilient. How would the corridor work? Instead of sending cargo entirely by sea from India to Europe through existing maritime routes, IMEC would combine shipping with overland rail connections. Goods from India would move by sea to the Gulf. From there, the proposed rail network would carry cargo across the Middle East towards the Mediterranean, where it could again move by sea into Europe. The plan also envisages supplementary road links and infrastructure for electricity, digital communications and clean energy. The Middle East Institute says the corridor could potentially reduce shipping times by up to 40% compared with traditional routes, although the eventual gains would depend on how much of the planned infrastructure is actually built and how efficiently the network operates. That multimodal design is also central to its strategic appeal: if one shipping route becomes vulnerable, cargo could have alternative land-based connections. Why has Trump linked IMEC to Iran? This is where the corridor has acquired a new significance. The Iran war has disrupted major energy and shipping routes across West Asia, including the Strait of Hormuz. Trump has argued that the region needs infrastructure that is less exposed to such chokepoints and to Iranian pressure. The proposed corridor is designed to provide an alternative route for goods and energy, although it would not simply replace the existing maritime system. Much of IMEC's infrastructure still has to be developed, and the route itself passes through a politically volatile region. The Middle East Institute notes that IMEC was originally designed to bypass vulnerable sections of the Bab al-Mandab and Suez routes through a combination of rail, ports, electricity grids and subsea cables. What does India gain? For India, IMEC is primarily about improving access to the Gulf and European markets while making supply chains more diversified. A functioning corridor could give Indian exporters another route into Europe and reduce their dependence on long maritime journeys. It could also deepen India's economic links with the UAE, Saudi Arabia and European economies. The planned digital infrastructure could connect India more closely with data networks in the Gulf and Europe, while the energy component could create new avenues for electricity and clean-energy cooperation. The corridor also fits into India's wider effort to expand its role in global connectivity and supply chains. Why isn't IMEC already operational? The biggest problem is geography, and geopolitics. The proposed route passes through a region that has been repeatedly hit by war and instability. The original concept also depended heavily on improved Saudi-Israeli ties and a stable connection through Israel and Jordan. The October 2023 Hamas attack and the wars that followed disrupted that political environment and slowed progress on the corridor. The Middle East Institute says the original form of IMEC is effectively on hold amid regional instability. There are also major infrastructure gaps. Rail links need to be developed or connected across several countries, while ports along the proposed route have different capacities and ownership structures. And there is competition. Other proposed routes, including the Iraq-Turkey-Europe Development Road, are also seeking to connect Asian and Middle Eastern markets with Europe. So Trump's endorsement does not mean IMEC is ready to start carrying cargo. The project still faces questions over funding, construction, regional security and political coordination. Why does IMEC matter now? When IMEC was announced in 2023, it was presented largely as a major trade and connectivity project linking India, the Gulf and Europe. The Iran war has given it another layer: route security. As wars and attacks expose the vulnerability of traditional energy and shipping chokepoints, the logic of having multiple routes for moving goods, energy and data has become more prominent. For India, that makes IMEC relevant not just as an infrastructure project but as a possible long-term alternative for connecting its economy with the Gulf and Europe. Trump's latest backing gives the project fresh political attention. Whether that translates into construction, however, will depend on whether the countries along the proposed route can overcome the geopolitical and infrastructure hurdles that have slowed IMEC since its launch. "I am honestly so grateful that you're here tonight with me. This concert is still a place where everyone is welcome and everyone here can stand beside people that have opposing views." title: BRICS New Delhi Declaration â persuasion works, not pressure
text: India hosts the 18th BRâICS Summit in New Delhi At a time of raging wars and a fragmenting world order, getting every BRICS member to agree on the New Delhi Declaration 2026 was no small feat. Consensus among countries frequently at odds with one another reflects India's credibility and the trust placed in it. India has done this once before, with the consensus declaration at the G20 in September 2023. The lesson at this BRICS summit is the same: countries that do not agree on everything can still work together. In a statement to fellow leaders, Prime Minister Narendra Modi put it plainly: BRICS is "not against anybody, but we take everybody forward with us." The original five members held divergent worldviews and political alignments, yet the clamour to join this non-Western grouping was such that its doors opened to six new members since 2024. Membership offers a way to protect strategic autonomy and, through multi-alignment, greater diplomatic leverage. That the world's biggest emerging economies and most populous countries, representing every major faith, should come together as the post-war rules-based order undergoes what Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney calls a "rupture", says something about where the global centre of gravity is shifting. The test now is what BRICS does with that weight. Its task is to help stabilise the world economy and to find alternatives to the weaponisation of trade, finance and technology. Its value lies in providing a table around which countries work on convergence instead of trading rhetoric. The conversations, however difficult, have to keep going. There is no shortage of agenda. The global financial system remains distorted, resting on a single dominant currency and a payments architecture controlled by the West, bent to political ends by the arbitrary tariffs of the past eighteen months. A BRICS currency would be a cure worse than the disease. Trade settled in national currencies is the more practical answer. It hedges against unilateral sanctions and builds confidence in national currencies. The India-UAE Local Currency Settlement System, launched in July 2023, already covers more than 11 per cent of bilateral trade and included a crude oil transaction worth $75 million in its first year. India and Russia have moved roughly 90 per cent of their bilateral payments into national currencies, amounting to $64.5 billion in 2024. Banks from more than 22 countries have opened Special Rupee Vostro Accounts to trade directly in rupees. Wars, some involving BRICS members, continue to take lives and damage the global economy, supply lines and energy security. India used the summit to urge members to keep trade, supply chains and energy flowing. In an unprecedented moment, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and UAE Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan met on the margins. A summit that convenes leaders is useful. One that builds bridges is more so. Members must also ensure that BRICS is not seen through an anti-West prism. The label was manufactured by sections of the Western press, amplified by capital-letter messages on Trumpâs Truth Social, and should not be allowed to stick. BRICS is neither a military alliance nor a treaty-based body. And there is irony in the charge. It was Western countries that went to war against one member, Iran, and imposed crippling sanctions on another, Russia. India's own record hardly suggests hostility. It has concluded trade agreements with the United Kingdom, EFTA, Australia and New Zealand, and wrapped up negotiations on the mother of all FTAs, with the European Union. Meanwhile, WTO non-compliant unilateral measures have been imposed by the United States on much of the world, and most sharply on BRICS countries. The rapid work of the BRICS Business Council deserves note. Shut out of the rich man's club that is the G7, it gives a platform to economies holding half the world's population, a quarter of world trade and 40 per cent of global GDP in purchasing power terms, and drawing a fifth of global foreign direct investment. Among them are the world's major energy producers and consumers, and much of its technological talent. The last decision of comparable interest to the Global South was the African Union's entry into the G20 during India's presidency in September 2023. The Global South will not be quieted, least of all by the shrillness coming from across the Atlantic. BRICS, as a grouping spread across three continents, gives confidence to the Global South that it matters. BRICS added South Africa, its S, in 2010 and is still in its teens, young and learning to navigate a turbulent world. It does not enjoy the advantages the G7 had from the mid-1970s, when a small, homogeneous set of countries came together around shared democratic values, advanced market capitalism and a common security umbrella. BRICS is a broad tent of different systems of government, economic structures, ideologies and faiths. What binds it is the desire for a multipolar order in which its members can develop and prosper, and in which they move from being rule-takers to rule-shapers. A successful summit leaves India with more room to manoeuvre and a larger part to play in keeping countries that often disagree in conversation. India is on the side not only of peace, but of prosperity and stability. (The author is former diplomat and Ambassador to the UAE) Disclaimer : Views expressed above are the author's own.

title: Andheri flyover repair faces second cost escalation, contract extension
text: Andheri flyover repair faces second cost escalation, contract extension Mumbai: A proposal seeking approval for a cost escalation in the Andheri flyover repair work will come up before the civic Standing Committee. The flyover on the Western Express Highway (WEH) is facing a second cost escalation and an extension of the contract period due to changes in the scope of work. The project cost has risen from the original amount of about Rs 93 crore to Rs 130 crore. Meanwhile, residents have questioned the time taken to complete the project. The repair work was initiated after a portion of a slab below the flyover fell on a car in July 2024. The work order for the flyover repairs was issued in October 2024. While the repair work was in progress, the technical adviser and VJTI were again requested to provide an extended methodology for carrying out the work. Accordingly, the technical adviser submitted the methodology to be adopted for the repairs, which was verified by VJTI. The methodology report stated that since the repair work on the bridge had started after at least 18 months, the superstructure of the bridge had become more fragile. Therefore, it was necessary to strengthen the diaphragm of the bridge. Accordingly, changes were made to the methodology for repairing the superstructure. The technical adviser pointed out that the changes resulted in an increase in the quantities in the Bill of Quantities (BOQ). Consequently, the contract amount for the original work, including the additional work, increased from about Rs 93 crore to about Rs 95 crore. While the repair work was in progress, vibrations were observed underneath the bridge and between the pillars when vehicles were moving over it. Public Works Department (PWD) was informed and requested to take necessary measures after conducting a structural examination of the bridge. However, in April 2025, PWD informed the civic body that the structural examination of the bridge should be carried out through VJTI and IIT Mumbai. According to the joint report of VJTI and IIT Mumbai, it was necessary to strengthen the columns and beams of the bridge. The report stated that otherwise, the main structure would be at risk and the possibility of loss of life could not be ruled out. An additional cost of Rs 11 crore was required to carry out the additional measures. Meanwhile, the state govt informed the civic body that it should carry out the repairs and raise the necessary funds on its own. Accordingly, the estimate for the additional strengthening of the columns and beams was put at about Rs 11 crore. Municipal Commissioner had earlier approved an extension of the contract period up to December 2025. However, due to the increase in the scope of the original work, it has now been proposed to extend the contract period up to November 2026. Dhaval Shah of Lokhandwala Oshiwara Citizens Association said that the flyover repair work had been delayed and should be completed on a war footing to ensure the safety and security of motorists and commuters. The civic body stated that the contract was awarded in 2024 at a cost of about Rs 93 crore. Thereafter, due to changes in the scope of the original work, the revised estimated cost after the first revision was about Rs 95 crore. The civic administration has now sought the approval of the civic Standing Committee for the revised cost of about Rs 130 crore after the second revision, as well as an extension of the contract period. title: Bangladesh to replace planned sculptures at historic sites
text: Bangladesh's Prime Minister Tarique Rahman DHAKA: The Tarique Rahman government has proposed replacing planned sculptures commemorating Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman's March 7, 1971 speech and the surrender of Pak forces the same year with water fountains at Suhrawardy Udyan. The proposal is part of a plan to "rescope and repurpose" the Independence Monument project, according to sources at ministry of liberation war affairs. Originally known as Ramna Race Course, Suhrawardy Udyan is a national memorial and public space located in Dhaka. The site, covering an area of 95 acres, is notably associated with two pivotal moments in Bangladeshi history: the historic speech by Sheikh Mujibur Rahman on 7 March, 1971, calling for struggle against the Pakistani establishment and the surrender of Pakistani forces on 16 Dec, 1971, which marked the end of the Bangladesh War of Independence. The project, titled "Construction of the Independence Monument at Suhrawardy Udyan in Dhaka", began in 2018 and is scheduled for completion in June 2027. title: Any terror attack originating from Pak soil will be considered an âAct of War': Rajnath
text: Rajnath Singh NEW DELHI: Defence minister Rajnath Singh said on Thursday that India articulated its new policy against terrorism through Op Sindoor, asserting that âany terror attack originating from Pakistani soil will be considered an âAct of Warâ against India and those contemplating any form of misadventure will be met with a response they deserve. " Speaking at News18 Defcon 2026, Rajnath said, âWeâve made it clear that the nation possesses both âpower of argumentâ and âargument of powerâ, and we will communicate through whichever language the other party understands best. Today, while we work towards establishing global peace through diplomacy, we are simultaneously strengthening our defence and strategic capabilities to counter any potential threat. Events such as surgical strikes , Balakot air strike, and Operation Sindoor demonstrated that we possess the necessary capability and resolve to safeguard our national interestsâ¦ India is a peace-loving nation that has never advocated for war. Yet, we must always remain prepared to safeguard our integrity & sovereignty, and protect our citizens.â India Opens DRDO Missile Technologies To Defence Firms In Major Push For Indigenous Production âTo view national security solely in terms of safeguarding geographical boundaries amounts to âperimeter fallacyâ,â Rajnath said as he reaffirmed Modi govtâs commitment to further bolster the countryâs defence preparedness and equip the military for emerging & future challenges. He emphasised that modern-day challenges encompass the use of drones and unmanned aerial vehicles, cyber-attacks, lone wolf attacks, and disinformation campaigns, in addition to the utilisation of arms and artillery by adversaries. He added that national security is linked to economic and energy security, and hostile actors may attempt to harm the economy or disrupt energy supply chains. âWeâve adopted a holistic approach to tackle these highly fluid threats,â he said. The minister enumerated the efforts taken by the govt to ensure strategic autonomy and national security while advancing towards the goal of Aatmanirbharta in defence. âThrough QUAD, weâre working towards a free, open, and rule-based Indo-Pacific. Through I2U2 (India, Israel, UAE and USA), weâve advanced cooperation in new areas. Our active participation in multilateral organisations such as BIMSTEC, BRICS, and SCO has also increased. Weâve strengthened strategic partnerships, created new platforms for cooperation, and expanded diplomatic reach on the global stage,â he explained. Describing âterrainâ, âtechnologyâ and âthinkingâ as the three Ts crucial to any war, Rajnath said that as new domains have emerged in modern warfare, the govt is focusing on technological development to tackle the challenges posed by the changing nature of warfare. He highlighted that military preparedness without diplomacy can lead to confrontation and a security dilemma, whereas proceeding solely on the basis of diplomacy, without requisite capability, is perceived as a sign of weakness and is detrimental to national security. He termed a balance between the two aspects as essential. âWeâve also conveyed the message that no border can prevent us from dismantling terrorist infrastructure. No distinction will be made between terrorists and their sponsors. By suspending the Indus Waters Treaty, weâve made it clear that blood and water cannot flow together. Our approach has now evolved beyond âstrategic containmentâ and âdeterrence by denialâ towards âdeterrence by punishmentâ,â he added. He noted that over the last 12 years, the allocation for defence research and development has increased by more than 112%, from Rs 13,700 crore in FY 2014-15 to over Rs 29,000 crore today. 25% of the defence R&D budget has been opened up for the industry, start-ups, and academia, enabling them to actively contribute to defence innovation, he added. He said over 5,500 items have, so far, been included across more than 10 positive indigenisation lists, demonstrating the emphasis on indigenous manufacturing of defence equipment and components that were previously imported.

title: Carpet cityâs new identity is Sant Ravidas Nagar Bhadohi, says CM
text: Varanasi: Chief minister Yogi Adityanath on Sunday said the carpet cityâs new identity is now Sant Ravidas Nagar Bhadohi. âOn the occasion of Guru Purnima , we had said that Bhadohi district, famous for its carpet industry, would in the coming time be known by the name of Satguru Ravidas Ji Maharaj, the medieval saint who united society,â Yogi said while addressing a public meeting at Bhikharipur Abhayanpur in Bhadohi after laying the foundation stone and inaugurating 112 projects worth Rs 1,340 crore. These include the inauguration of 65 projects worth Rs 440 crore and the foundation-laying of 47 projects worth Rs 899 crore. He said Sant Ravidas Ji Maharaj had envisioned an ideal society through his words: âI desire such a kingdom where everyone gets food, where the small and the big live equally, and Raidas remains happy.â âUnder the leadership of Prime Minister Narendra Modi , more than 80 crore people in the country are receiving the benefit of free ration and many other benefits. In this context, naming the district Sant Ravidas Nagar Bhadohi is appropriate,â said Yogi. In 1994, the Mulayam Singh Yadav govt created Bhadohi district by separating its area from Varanasi district. A political tug-of-war over its name started in 1997 when, after coming to power, Bahujan Samaj Party chief Mayawati renamed the district Sant Ravidas Nagar. However, as carpet industrialists and exporters had concerns over an identity crisis for their product, which had a brand name as Bhadohi carpet, BJP chief minister late Ram Prakash Gupta in 1999 took note of it and changed the name of the district to Sant Ravidas Nagar Bhadohi. This decision upset the Samajwadi Party, and after returning to power in 2012, the Akhilesh Yadav government restored the districtâs name to Bhadohi in 2014. But when the BJP, which focused on developing the 15th-century poet-saint and Dalit icon Sant Ravidas at Seer Gowardhanpur in Varanasi, intensified its Dalit outreach programme, especially after the SPâs PDA formula worked against it in the 2024 Lok Sabha election and Uttar Pradesh approached the 2027 assembly election, the renaming was ensured. CM Yogi, along with BJP national chief Nitin Nabin and state president Pankaj Chaudhary, on the occasion of Guru Purnima on July 29, flagged off the âShri Guru Ravidas Maharaj Samrasta Sankalp Abhiyanâ in Varanasi to mark the 650th Prakash Parv of Sant Ravidas, which will conclude on the occasion of the saintâs birth anniversary on Maghi Purnima on February 20, 2027. On the same day, Yogi had announced the renaming of Bhadohi as Sant Ravidas Nagar Bhadohi. title: 'World is getting worse': Antonio Guterres warns wars, divisions are paralysing UN
text: Antonio Guterres told reporters the need for stronger oversight would be a major focus of his talks with global leaders coming to the city. UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres has warned that the global situation is deteriorating as wars spread and become increasingly complicated, with deep divisions among major powers leaving the Security Council unable to respond effectively to growing crises. Speaking to Al Jazeera on Monday, a day before delivering his final address to the UN General Assembly as secretary-general, Guterres said the world body was facing serious challenges over its ability to deal with conflicts and uphold international law. 'Environment of impunity' Guterres said the involvement of major powers and permanent members of the UN Security Council in conflicts had made it harder for the council to act. He said repeated violations of international law were contributing to a broader sense that countries could act without facing consequences. Watch 'If Trump Violates Law Once More...': UN Chief Guterres' Explosive Warning To U.S. Before UNGA "That creates an environment of impunity, in which midsize powers believe that they can do whatever they want because nothing will happen to them," Guterres said. According to the UN chief, geopolitical divisions have effectively paralysed the Security Council at a time when the number of conflicts is growing. He warned that the consequences were being felt most severely by vulnerable populations caught up in wars and economic disruption. Wars driving food and fuel costs Guterres pointed to the Russia-Ukraine war and the US-Israel war on Iran as conflicts with consequences far beyond the countries directly involved. He said disruptions to food, fertiliser and energy supplies were adding to pressure on economies around the world. Problems affecting key maritime routes, including the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb, have further complicated the movement of energy and goods. "The combination of the war in Ukraine with the problems of exports of foods, fertilisers, and energy through the Black Sea, if you combine it with the difficulties in the Strait of Hormuz [in the Gulf], in the Bab al-Mandeb [in the Red Sea], and in the attacks [on] oil installations in several countries of the [Middle East] region, we are creating a situation that has a devastating impact on many economies around the world," Guterres said. He said wealthier countries could eventually absorb higher interest rates and energy costs, but developing nations faced much greater difficulties. People in poorer countries, he said, were being pushed into "a desperate situation" as food and energy became more expensive and access to fertilisers became harder. UN faces pressure to reform Guterres, a former prime minister of Portugal and former UN high commissioner for refugees, has led the organisation since January 1, 2017. His second term ends on December 31, 2026, after which a new secretary-general will take charge. Guterres said his successor would inherit a UN facing multiple conflicts and a growing gap between the scale of global challenges and the organisation's ability to respond. He argued that reforms would be necessary if the UN is to remain an effective and relevant institution in a world increasingly divided by geopolitical rivalries.
